news.title: GOP Rep. Insists He's Not LGBTQ+ After Releasing Flirty Text Messages He Received From Men
news.text:
Congressman-elect Anthony Constantino has vowed to turn every g-y American into a Republican, claiming the Democratic Party has made it "unsafe to be G-y" while arguing that GOP positions on border security, public safety, taxes, and gun rights should appeal to LGBTQ+ voters, RadarOnline.com can report.

The New York Republican made the declaration on social media on November 23, sharing purported private messages from men who appeared to express both political support and romantic interest.Anthony Constantino’s Outreach PledgeConstantino first announced his recruitment effort in a video posted on November 22, promising to provide more details about his plans. 

He followed up on November 23 with another video, again declaring his intention to get every g-y American to join the Republican Party without explaining how he planned to accomplish the goal.

"Hey American, everybody wants to know how I’m gonna turn every gay American Republican. It’s easy. Watch," he said before breaking into an in-car karaoke performance of Stevie Wonder’s 1980 song Master Blaster (Jammin’).

The incoming congressman also shared what appeared to be screenshots of private messages from men expressing interest in his political views.

"You turned me Republican," one message read, while another offered, "S-xy, let me know if you want to play."Constantino Said Mamdani Doesn't Like The LGBTQ+Constantino also directed his criticism toward New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, making unsubstantiated claims that the mayor had deceived g-y voters and that Muslims privately mocked them for supporting Democrats.

"It makes no sense that any G-y American wants to be in the Party of Mamdani," Constantino wrote.

"These Muslims are LAUGHING AT YOU. They think G-ys are stupid for voting for Democrats," he continued, making further claims about Mamdani's visits to Uganda.LGBTQ+ Voters Backed Kamala Harris in 2024Constantino's recruitment campaign comes as voting data show that LGBTQ+ Americans overwhelmingly supported the Democratic presidential ticket in the last election.

Kamala Harris received 86 percent of LGBTQ+ voters' support in the 2024 presidential election, compared with 12 percent for President Donald Trump, according to a report.

Democrats experienced a wave of LGBTQ+ electoral victories during the midterm elections, including Sen.-elect Chris Pappas of New Hampshire.

Constantino, who defeated Democratic challenger Blake Gendebien in New York's 21st Congressional District, will take office after replacing former Rep. Elise Stefanik.Anthony Constantino Reveals Text MessagesConstantino shared what appeared to be screenshots of his private inbox, featuring messages from men who expressed interest in his political views and, in some cases, appeared to flirt with the incoming congressman.

"Please red pill me as a g-y man sir," one message read, while another said, "You turned me republican.”

Other messages were decidedly less political.

"You're really handsome," one person wrote, while another offered, "S-xy, let me know if you want to play…"

"It's already begun. I want to clarify, I am not G-y but I do want all Gay Americans to become Republican," Constantino wrote alongside the screenshot. "The Democrat Party is making it unsafe to be G-y."

Constantino has also drawn attention for his unconventional approach to political messaging, previously pleading with Trump to release Sean 'Diddy' Combs.
news.summary: Anthony Constantino insisted he is not LGBTQ+ after releasing flirty text messages he says he received from men.

news.title: How Democrats are gaming out the timing of their 2028 bids: From the Politics Desk
news.text: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail. In today’s edition, Natasha Korecki explores when we might see Democratic presidential contenders launch their campaigns. Plus, Sahil Kapur interviews DSCC Chair Kirsten Gillibrand about the 2028 Senate map. Programming note: We are taking a holiday break the rest of the week and will be back in your inbox on Monday. Have a happy Thanksgiving! — Adam Wollner How Democrats are gaming out the timing of their 2028 bids Analysis by Natasha Korecki Now that the midterm elections are all of three weeks behind us, Democratic White House hopefuls can get real about their 2028 campaigns. With that comes one of the first big decisions they’ll need to make: exactly when to enter the race. Jump in early and face the harsh national spotlight and a possibility of burning through cash too soon. Wait too long and risk getting left behind in what’s expected to be a crowded field. We talked to advisers to potential candidates, donors and outside strategists who laid out the major considerations that go into deciding the right moment to officially announce a campaign for president. Here are some of the key factors to keep an eye on. A mad rush in two phases: Several strategists said to expect to see two main phases of rollouts (with the potential of it starting even before the end of the year). The first is in January, after the new party superstars in Congress settle in. And the second is in February and March, with the bulk of the field likely to be in place by March 31, just as the first quarter of fundraising ends. “The minute you jump in, you need to start paying people, raising money, all of those things,” a senior Democratic strategist who worked on a presidential campaign in 2020 said. “But time is also your friend in a crowded field. … You need to distinguish yourself.” Governing: Voters just re-elected Govs. Josh Shapiro in Pennsylvania, JB Pritzker in Illinois and Gov. Wes Moore in Maryland to four-year-terms. It’s unlikely they’d announce before their own January swearing-in ceremonies. And they might even have to clear legislative sessions and state of the state addresses from their plates first. Money: Locking down donors is vital to demonstrate fundraising strength early. Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear is asking his donors to convene in December before any decision happens. Some potential contenders, like Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly, are already sitting on a pile of cash. And while Pritzker, a notorious self-financier, is expected to fundraise for the first time, the billionaire can reliably lean on personal wealth. Staffing up: Some nascent campaigns have already locked down their hired guns, but with so many Democrats competing for talent, there are some potential contenders still wrangling over some important hires. “There are a lot of factors,” said a person working with a potential 2028 candidate. “It’s a conversation I know everybody is having.” Book releases: Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg is due out with a book in January. Moore has a scheduled March release for his book. Conventional wisdom (though it isn’t always accurate) is that candidates will seek to tap into momentum from the publishing tours to then shift into campaign mode. The X factors: As we reported this week, what Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., and former Vice President Kamala Harris decide to do looms particularly large over the rest of the field. Someone like Rep. Ro Khanna may want to jump in sooner rather than later to get a leg up in the progressive lane over AOC. For his part, California Gov. Gavin Newsom has said he would not run for president if Harris does — though not everyone is buying that. “When he said it, it was total bull----,” said billionaire Democratic donor John Morgan. “Put this down for my prediction: Even if she runs, he’s running.” 🔵 Related: Democrats grumble about the DNC’s plan for the 2028 primary debates, by Jonathan Allen and Natasha Korecki DSCC chair says it’s ‘definitely possible’ for Democrats to win 60 Senate seats in 2028 By Sahil Kapur Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y. is seeking another two-year term as chair of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee after her party flipped nine seats on its way to securing a 56-seat majority. In an interview with NBC News, Gillibrand said she’s bullish that Democrats can expand the map again in 2028, calling it “definitely possible” to capture 60 seats and win a very rare, filibuster-proof majority. “It’s on the table. There’s some easy targets that I’m very excited about — obviously, Wisconsin and North Carolina,” Gillibrand said. “But I would also suggest any state that was in play last cycle is in play this cycle. Waves tend to be two cycles long, and this is a very large blue tsunami.” If Democrats hold all their seats in 2028, their best pickup opportunities are seats in the highly competitive states of Wisconsin (held by Sen. Ron Johnson) and North Carolina (held by Sen. Ted Budd). From there the hill gets steeper, requiring victories in redder states. “I think we can put a lot of these states that we put in play last time that are exciting states like Kansas and South Carolina and Iowa,” all of which Democrats won in November, Gillibrand said. “There’s no reason why we can’t find extraordinary candidates, again, who have the right message to fight for their states to run in these very red and purple places.” Read more → That’s all From the Politics Desk for now. Today’s newsletter was compiled by Adam Wollner. If you have feedback — likes or dislikes — email us at politicsnewsletter@nbcuni.com And if you’re a fan, please share with everyone and anyone. They can sign up here.
news.summary: In today’s edition, Natasha Korecki explores when we might see Democratic presidential contenders launch their campaigns.

news.title: Nolte: Mean Girls at ‘Vanity Fair’ Rip Taylor Swift for Political Reasons
news.text:
These days, everything can be answered through a political lens because everything has been politicized by Democrats. For example: Why would the far-left Vanity Fair publish a hit piece on Taylor Swift that’s so poorly and thinly sourced, and in which her name is never used?

If you’ve read the piece, and I have, you might ask yourself another question… Why does Vanity Fair angle the article as a hit piece when even the worst behavior it alleges about Taylor Swift makes her look awesome?

It is, admittedly, a nicely composed piece and structured using the conceit of record sides. SIDE A is the myth around Taylor Swift. SIDE B is the supposed truth about Taylor Swift. This is an interesting approach when no one under 40 will get the reference.

According to Vanity Fair, Swift’s career was launched due to her own ambition which was backed by her equally ambitious parents and the fact they are wealthy. What’s more, over the course of her legendary career, Swift has feuded with fellow artists, used her relationships with various guys as recording material, and she can be equal parts shrewd and ruthless in her business dealings.

Sometimes, in both her music and business dealings, she allegedly twists the truth to make herself look more like the victim.

Sometimes she’s exceedingly generous to fellow musicians, especially women.

Sometimes, if she perceives a slight, she cuts them off entirely.

Honestly, that’s the worst Vanity Fair could find after talking to dozens of people about a woman in the public spotlight for more than 20 years. All I came away with was the impression that she’s ambitious, has no tolerance for bullshit, and doesn’t take any crap. In other words, she’s an American.

And so what if her parents have money? Do you know how many stage parents with money have wasted all that money on a talentless child?

Mommy and Daddy’s money only gets you so far.

Listen, I’m no Swiftie. I’m not even a music guy. Preferring silence, I don’t turn on the radio during long drives. But I still see Taylor Swift as an insanely talented, wildly ambitious, ridiculously successful, and slightly neurotic pop superstar who — within the context of pop superstars — is probably the healthiest example of a pop culture superstar America has seen in decades.

Yes, she’s a little self-involved. Yes, she was pretty partisan for a short time (only after being bullied into it). But look at the upside: no tattoos, no nose rings, no arrests, no sex tape, no paparazzi meltdowns. In the face of an Elvis-sized fame that began when she was still a teenager, Taylor Swift has shown remarkable poise and class. And she’s a girly-girl without any of the heavy hyper-sexualization that has defined pop music for decades.

So why is Vanity Fair straining to pretend it has uncovered damaging information about her, such as the fact she owned three pairs of Uggs in high school? (Seriously, that’s in the story.)

Well, Swift has toned down speaking out about politics — her endorsement of Kamala Harris was tepid at best. She’s also begun releasing songs about the joys of being a wife, suburban life, and having babies…

I just want you (You, you, yeah), huh
Have a couple kids, got the whole block looking like you
We tell the world to leave us the fuck alone, and they do (Ooh), wow
Got me dreaming ’bout a driveway with a basketball hoop (Hoop)
Boss up, settle down, got a wish (Wish) list (List)

And so, the Vanity Fair article is a classic (and predictable) piece of media bullying against a high-profile celebrity who’s looking like she might color outside of the accepted political and social lines. Shame on Taylor Swift for not holding concerts for Kamala Harris, for maturing and realizing not all men are evil.

What I wrote in her defense last year still stands:

For going on 20 years, Swift had been the goddess who affirmed their lonely, bitter, anti-male lifestyle. She was all about her career, all about wrist-flicking the patriarchy, all about the narcissism of self-care.
But unlike these former worshipers (who are mostly homely, bitter, and impossible to live with), Taylor Swift has options. She’s rich and beautiful, which means she has a banquet of desirable men laid out before her. She’s also smart enough to grow up and grasp the idea that being alone and childless at 40 is no way to live.

In another lyric, Swift admitted, “I like my friends cancelled.”

The fascists at Vanity Fair will never stand by and do nothing in the face of Based Taylor Swift.
news.summary:
Why does "Vanity Fair" angle an article as a hit piece when even the worst behavior it alleges about Taylor Swift makes her look awesome?

news.title: Sen. Deb Fischer’s husband dies
news.text:
The husband of Sen. Deb Fischer of Nebraska died over the weekend, the lawmaker said in a statement.Details of the death of Bruce Fischer on Sunday were not shared in the statement, but the senator said that her husband died “doing what he loved most, spending time outdoors.” Bruce Fischer was a cattle rancher.

The Fischers married in 1972, while the lawmaker was a student at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln. news.title: Democrats turn sights to 2028 after US midterms triumph
news.text: WASHINGTON, D.C. — Democrats on Monday fired the starting gun on the race to win back the White House, announcing plans for 12 debates to pick their standard bearer for 2028 as the party looks to build on its sweeping midterm election victory.The first debate is scheduled for June next year, setting the stage for what could be a crowded contest to select a challenger to the Republicans, who must find a successor to term-limited President Donald Trump.The announcement comes as Democrats celebrate their biggest majority in the House of Representatives since the early 1990s, with their victories this month transforming the balance of power in Washington and raising expectations for the next two years.“Democrats are on offense after our historic victories in the midterms, and the DNC is keeping our foot on the gas as we head into the 2028 cycle,” Democratic National Committee chairman Ken Martin said.The party will hold five debates in 2027 and seven in 2028, the final one scheduled for March of that year.The televised showdowns will help voters choose the party’s presidential nominee through a series of state-by-state primary elections and caucuses, in which supporters select the candidate they want to face the Republican nominee in November 2028.Crowded fieldUnder new rules announced Monday, candidates seeking a place on the debate stage must pledge to denounce spending on their behalf by outside political groups, including those that do not disclose their donors.The requirement is intended to curb the influence of wealthy donors and so-called dark money in Democratic nomination contests, a longstanding demand of the party’s progressive wing.No major Democrat has formally entered the race, but maneuvering is already underway among politicians seeking to become the party’s next leader.Gavin Newsom, Josh Shapiro and Andy Beshear — the governors of California, Pennsylvania and Kentucky, respectively — are among those attracting attention as possible contenders.Other names being discussed include former vice president Kamala Harris, defeated by Trump in 2024; former transportation secretary Pete Buttigieg; and New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a leading figure on the party’s left.Sen. Jon Ossoff of Georgia — seen as one of the party’s rising stars — have also been mentioned as potential candidates, along with Sen. Cory Booker of New Jersey.The sprawling field reflects a party debating its direction after Trump’s reelection in 2024, with moderates and progressives offering competing visions of how to recapture the presidency.But Democrats enter the contest buoyed by an extraordinary midterm performance that handed them control of both chambers of Congress.Historic majorityThe party has secured at least 258 seats in the 435-member House, its largest majority since 1992, with several races still outstanding.Democrats will also control 56 seats in the 100-member Senate when the new Congress convenes in January.Hakeem Jeffries, who was nominated last week to lead the House Democrats, is poised to become the first Black speaker when lawmakers formally elect their leader on Jan. 3.The election has also strengthened the Congressional Black Caucus, whose membership is expected to grow despite Republican efforts to redraw congressional districts following a Supreme Court ruling weakening voting rights protections.Black lawmakers are set to occupy several prominent House leadership positions and committee chairmanships, while the incoming Senate will have seven Black members, including three women — both historic highs.Democrats have promised an ambitious legislative program focused on lowering living costs, reversing Republican healthcare cuts and investigating alleged corruption within Trump’s administration.But their new congressional strength comes with limitations, as Trump retains the power to veto legislation, while most major bills require 60 votes to overcome procedural obstacles in the Senate.

news.title: JD Vance’s Wipeout Excuse Torpedoed in Brutal Reality Check
news.text:
“Our voters did show up,” the vice president wrote on X, in a claim echoed by Sen. Ted Cruz. “But the main problem is not turnout. The main problem is that many people who voted for Trump/Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026.”

But a Washington Post analysis of 13 Senate races suggests Vance got it badly wrong.

According to the Post, the biggest reason for the Democratic surge was not hordes of Trump voters defecting to the other side but Republicans failing to turn out while Democrats flooded the polls.

The findings suggest that most Democratic gains, around 70 percent, came from changes in who turned out to vote, rather than people changing their political allegiance. 

Only around 20 percent came from voters switching parties, with the rest explained by new voters and those moving away from third-party candidates.

For every 100 people who voted for Donald Trump in 2024, roughly 33 stayed home, while between one and eight crossed over to vote Democrat, depending on the state.

That finding is supported by national exit polls, which found that 7 percent of Trump voters backed Democrats, compared with just 2 percent of Kamala Harris voters who supported Republicans.

The biggest difference was how successfully each party held on to its existing supporters.

Republicans retained 64 percent of Trump’s 2024 voters across the races examined, broadly in line with historical midterm patterns. Democrats held on to 92 percent of Harris voters, far above the usual 68 to 81 percent range for the party out of power.

That suggests the Democratic wave was driven less by an extraordinary Republican revolt than by Democrats keeping their own supporters engaged while attracting some additional voters.

There were, however, several states where switching sides played a much bigger role.

Texas offered the starkest example. Trump carried the state by nearly 14 points in 2024, yet Democrat James Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton for a U.S. Senate seat by 12 points.

About 8 percent of Trump’s previous supporters backed Talarico, the highest share among the states analyzed by the Post. The findings also suggested that switching was particularly common in heavily Hispanic areas.

In Hidalgo County, which is more than 90 percent Hispanic, most of the Democratic gains were attributed to former Trump voters backing Talarico.

Georgia and South Carolina also showed evidence of significant crossover voting.

In South Carolina, Democrat Annie Andrews defeated Darline Graham by four points in the race for Graham’s late brother’s longtime Senate seat, representing a 22-point swing from the 2024 presidential result. Around a third of the Democratic gains came from former Trump voters.

Georgia, meanwhile, showed how powerful turnout could be. Around a third of Trump’s 2024 supporters stayed home, but Democrats were particularly successful at attracting new voters.

Some 420,000 Georgians who had not voted in 2024 turned out this year. Relative to the number of previous voters, they were about twice as common in heavily Democratic precincts as in heavily Republican ones.

However, the Democratic gains were less dramatic in parts of the North, including Michigan and Minnesota, and that is because Republicans held onto more of their voters in those states.

Democrats won both states, but their margins were smaller than the wider national swing might have suggested. Republicans held on to 72 percent of Trump’s voters in Michigan and 77 percent in Minnesota, well above the 60 percent average across the 13 states.

There was even evidence of voters moving in the opposite direction. In Michigan, about 96,000 Harris voters switched to Republicans, compared with 40,000 Trump voters who backed Democrats. 

Minnesota showed a similar pattern, with about 24,000 more Harris voters switching to Republicans than Trump voters moving to the Democrats.

The Daily Beast has contacted Vance’s office for comment.
news.summary:

After Democrats stormed back take control of Congress in the 2026 midterms, Republicans have been scrambling to explain their losses, with the vice president insisting the party’s supporters had turned out but voted Democrat instead.

“Our voters did show up,” the vice president wrote on X, in a claim echoed by Sen. Ted Cruz. “But the main problem is not turnout. The main problem is that many people who voted for Trump/Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026.”

news.title: EXPLAINED: France's strict rules on election campaign funding
news.text:
Presidential campaigns in France are subject to strict financing rules - and candidates who break them face serious legal consequences, up to and including jail time.

Here's how the French system works;

Spending is capped

The amount of money that candidates can spend during a presidential election is subject to strict limits.

French candidates are currently limited to a total campaign spend of €22.51 million. 

This limit covers the one-year period before the election - so for the 2027 election it started in April 2026.

All candidates can spend up to €16.85 million until the date of the first round of the election, which is April 18th, 2027.

The two top-polling candidates then go through to a second round - they're allowed to spend an additional €5.66 million in the two-week period between round one and round two.

By contrast, Kamala Harris and Donald Trump raised and spent an estimated combined total of over $5.5 billion on their 2024 US election campaigns. 

French spending caps are also significantly lower than those imposed in the UK, where nationwide general election campaign spending is limited to £34 million.

Donor limits

As well as the overall spending ceiling, there are limits on who candidates can accept money from - donations from businesses or legal entities (including lobby groups or charities) are 100 percent banned.

When it comes to donations from individuals, they are capped at €4,600 per person, so super-wealthy individuals cannot buy political influence through donations.

Cash payments are limited to €150 - and candidates are required to keep detailed records of who gives them money.

The geographical origin of donations matters too. A law passed after the 2017 election decreed that candidates could no longer borrow money from financial organisations based outside of the European Economic Area (EEA).

This meant that Marine Le Pen's January 2022 loan of more than €10 million from a bank in Hungary was legal - whereas loans from Russian banks, which her party had previously used to finance earlier campaigns, were no longer permitted.

All candidates who make it onto the ballot paper must also make a declaration disclosing their assets and wealth and declaring their financial interests and professional activities, as well as those of their spouses.

These déclarations de patrimoine are very detailed - so for example in 2022 we learned that the highest value possession of Trotskyist candidate Philippe Poutou was his car, a Peugeot 308.

Government funding

There is, however, another source of funding - the state.

All candidates on the ballot paper for round one receive €200,000 of public money to campaign.

French presidential candidates who win more than 5 percent of the vote in the first round can then receive up to €8 million in government reimbursements to cover their campaign costs. Those who win less than 5 percent only get up to €800,423 reimbursed by the state.

Candidates who make it through to the second round can have up to €10.7 million reimbursed by the state.

Campaign expenses don’t include advertising

Expenses that are eligible for state reimbursement include public meetings and rallies, campaign materials, headquarters and staff salaries. 

Candidates can also submit expenses for ‘digital campaigning’, which includes the cost of developing, hosting and maintaining official websites and mobile apps. Video and podcast production, as well as graphic content creation are also covered.

However, paid commercial ads on TV, radio, print newspapers, billboards, search engines, or sponsored social media posts during the 6 months prior to the election are strictly prohibited by law and are not, therefore, counted as expenses. 

Instead, French candidates receive free, allocated public airtime, where they promote their campaign message.

Other prohibited expenses in France include campaign bills paid directly by the candidate, a supporter or a third party; personal expenses such as clothing, medical care, cosmetics, or private living costs; parking tickets and tax penalties; and lavish private social receptions unrelated to public election meetings.

The biggest spenders usually win

Historical examples suggest that spending up to the maximum is worth it.

Emmanuel Macron beat Marine Le Pen in the second round of the 2022 presidential election, after outspending her by roughly €6.03 million - a repeat of what happened in the 2017 presidential election, when he spent €4 million more than her. 

Nicolas Sarkozy won the 2007 presidential election after outspending his rivals and Chirac won the 1995 and 2002 elections as the biggest spender.

One recent exception is the 2012 election in which Nicolas Sarkozy lost to François Hollande in the second round despite spending more money. That year, Sarkozy didn't receive any reimbursement from the state to cover campaign costs after breaching the spending limit. He was officially left with close to €23 million to cover himself.

Campaign accounts are centralised and monitored

Candidates are not allowed to directly collect donations or pay campaign expenses. Instead, all candidates on the official list must declare a campaign account, which is managed by a financial agent, which can be an individual or an electoral financing association.

This account details income, expenses, in-kind contributions, supporting documents (including invoices and examples of campaign materials such as leaflets), and transactions in the agent's bank account.

The Commission nationale des comptes de campagne et des financements politiques (CNCCFP) monitors the campaign accounts and political financing of candidates in French elections. 

Those who break the rules face heavy (albeit often delayed) penalties

If the CNCCFP finds irregularities in a candidate's campaign accounts, it can ask judicial authorities to launch an investigation.

The most famous example of someone who has fallen foul of this system is former president Nicolas Sarkozy.

In 2021, a court sentenced Sarkozy to one year in prison (later reduced to six months with an electronic tag, which a judge waived in May 2026 due to his age), for spending close to double the legal limit during his failed attempt to win re-election in 2012.

The case was known as the Bygmalion affair, after the name of the public relations firm hired by Sarkozy to orchestrate a blitz of lavish US-style election rallies. Executives of the firm admitted to using a system of fake invoices to mask the real cost of the events.

news.title: My Turn: Tax the rich. Fund public education. Win elections.
news.text:
One of Wallace Steven’s most famous poems is “Thirteen Ways of Looking at a Blackbird.” I’ve come back repeatedly to the fifth stanza:

I do not know which to prefer,The beauty of inflectionsOr the beauty of innuendoes,The blackbird whistlingOr just after. 

We just had an election of monumental importance. And now the stories get told about what it meant. The election was the “inflection.” What we make of it is the “innuendo.”

The poet insists he does “not know which to prefer.” In politics, we have no choice but to look forward, to tell the story and to shape the “innuendoes.”

One key lesson from the beautifully unexpected repudiation of President Donald Trump and his lapdog enablers in the Party of Trump and in the billionaire class is that fighting to retake the country from the wealthy in order to fund public education, a core common good, is a recipe for electoral victory.

Look at the shocking victories in Texas. Gina Hinojosa, who will be the first Latina governor in the history of Texas, was inspired to run, and made as a foundation of her campaign, the fight for public schools. She beat Gov. Greg Abbott, who was seen as unbeatable only days before the election. James Talarico was a public school teacher who built his reputation in the Texas legislature as a defender of public education and became an outspoken opponent of Abbott and the Republican Party’s decimation of public education through private school vouchers and public school funding cuts. 

Dozens of other candidates in states across the country made investing in public education— and protecting it from private school voucher schemes that are designed to crush the very idea of universal, free, public education — a key plank. The Prop 3 referendum to make permanent a tax on millionaires to fund public education passed almost 60-40 in California. Meanwhile, the Prop 40 California wealth tax, which was focused on protecting healthcare, was opposed by the $300 million of a few billionaires, suffered from a lack of funds and division in the labor coalition, and ultimately failed.

Washington voters soundly rejected an attempt by the very rich to roll back the millionaire’s tax, modeled on our own Fair Share Amendment, which will benefit public education. Here in Massachusetts, we rejected the second of two attempts to undermine the Fair Share Amendment, the 2024 amendment to our Constitution that is bringing in over $3 billion a year from the wealthiest residents of the commonwealth. Those efforts were led by the Mass High Tech Council, Pioneer Institute and Competitiveness Council. They resent that we, the citizens of Massachusetts, are “calling back,” in the words of our Amherst permanent poet laureate, Emily Dickinson, about $3 billion a year to fund everything from more childcare, to universal school meals, to free higher education and better roads and bridges and public transportation. One of those efforts was thrown out by the Supreme Judicial Court, the other by the voters on Nov. 3.

And this is hardly new. Look back to the 2024 election. In Kentucky, Trump beat Kamala Harris by 30 points. But those same voters, on the same ballot, voted by the exact same margin to reject private school vouchers. In Nebraska, where Trump won about 60% of the vote, vouchers were rejected 57-42. You can’t achieve that result unless many of the voters who voted to return Trump to the White House also rejected one of his and the Republicans’ central — and maybe their only — public education policy: diverting public money to private and religious schools. 

When I was president of the Massachusetts Teachers Association and traveling almost daily up to Gloucester during the educator strike (which was illegal in Massachusetts, incidentally) in November 2024, I was struck by a house at the bottom of the off-ramp from Route 1. On one column of the front porch was a MAGA “Make America Great Again” sign. And on the other column was a sign with this message: “Support the Union of Gloucester Educators.” People can gravitate toward conservative candidates who appear populist, but they care deeply about the public schools and public school educators to which they entrust their children. 

And they want to tax the very rich, to take back some of their ungodly power to purchase elected officials and policies that benefit the rich and to invest in the things voters care about, most centrally public education. A recent poll by Hart Research, which was commissioned by Better Taxes for a Better America, found that 85% of voters felt that the wealthy should be taxed more. That number beat out the response to questions about whether or not the Earth is round and if apple pie is tasty. In other words, we have a near-universal consensus that the wealthy need to pay their fair share, as long as the money is invested in what matters most, and public education is at the top of the list. 

We are at an inflection point. Let the “innuendoes” from this election make their way into the public policy platforms of 2028 and beyond.

Max Page is a professor of architecture at the University of Massachusetts Amherst.

news.title: 'I'm Not Gay': GOP Rep.-Elect Launches Campaign To 'Get Every Gay American To Be Republican'
news.text:
Rep.-elect Anthony Constantino (R-N.Y.) bizarrely shared purported thirsty messages from “gay Americans” as proof that his drive to recruit them to the Republican Party is working.

“It’s already begun,” he wrote Monday on X. “I want to clarify, I am not Gay but I do want all Gay Americans to become Republican. The Democrat Party is making it unsafe to be Gay. If you like Secure Borders, Safety, Low Taxes, Less Regulation, as well as First and Second Amendment Rights then you should be Republican.”

“You turned me Republican,” one comment read. “Sexy, let me know if you want to play,” went another.

Constantino, who is replacing Elise Stefanik in the upstate district, also targeted New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani in an Islamophobic rant that baselessly claimed Mamdani had “conned Gays.”

“It makes no sense that any Gay American wants to be in the Party of Mamdani,” he wrote. “These Muslims are LAUGHING AT YOU. They think Gays are stupid for voting for Democrats. This is all Zohran talks about when he goes to Uganda. He giggles like Hyena about the FACT that he conned Gays.”

HuffPost has reached out to Mamdani’s office for comment.

Constantino said in a short video on Sunday his goal was to “get every gay American to be Republican. More on this soon.”

He followed with a similar pledge Monday ― again without details of his supposed outreach.

“Hey American, everybody wants to know how I’m gonna turn every gay American Republican. It’s easy. Watch,” he began.

Constantino then did a bit of in-car karaoke to Stevie Wonder’s 1980 song “Master Blaster (Jammin’).”

“We’ve agreed to get together, joined as children in Jah,” the incoming lawmaker sang in his X post. “When you’re moving in the positive, your destination is the brightest star.” 

Constantino will have his work cut out for him. Within the blue wave that crushed Republicans in the midterm was a Democratic rainbow wave of LGBTQ+ winners, led by Sen.-elect Chris Pappas (N.H.).

As for the electorate: Even amid President Donald Trump’s victory in 2024, Democrat Kamala Harris still dominated him 86% to 12% among LGBTQ voters, NBC reported.

news.title: New York congressman-elect on crusade to make gay Americans Republican
news.text:
Representative-elect Anthony Constantino of New York says he wants to persuade gay Americans to join the Republican Party. The incoming congressman, whose first posts about the effort drew flirtatious messages on social media, has since clarified that he is not gay while continuing to promote his political appeal.

In a video posted to X on November 21, Constantino said: “Now that I’m elected, one of my big goals is to get every gay American to be Republican.” He did not provide details in the video but promised to say more about the effort soon.

Constantino later shared what appeared to be screenshots of private messages, with the senders’ names obscured. Some were flirtatious, with one saying, “You turned me republican.” Constantino posted publicly in response, “I am not Gay but I do want all Gay Americans to become Republican.”

Constantino continued: “The Democrat Party is making it unsafe to be Gay. If you like Secure Borders, Safety, Low Taxes, Less Regulation, as well as First and Second Amendment Rights then you should be Republican.”

In a statement to Newsweek, Jeremy Comeau, the president of the National Federation of Stonewall Democrats, said: “As for the claim that Democrats are making it unsafe to be gay, LGBTQ people know exactly who has been writing the laws aimed at us, and it isn’t Democrats. Republicans have spent years passing bills that target transgender Americans, pushing to roll back marriage equality, and turning our lives into campaign attack ads. You don’t get to light the fire and then sell us the extinguisher.

“The data isn’t close. LGBTQ voters backed Democrats by 86 percent in this month’s exit polls. That isn’t blind party loyalty. It’s a reaction to what Republicans have actually done. If Republicans truly want to earn gay votes, the path is simple. Stop legislating against trans people. Put marriage equality protections into law and keep them there. Support the Equality Act. Protect funding for HIV prevention and care. Until that happens, no post from a congressman-elect is going to change the math.”

Comeau’s 86 percent figure matches reported 2024 presidential exit-poll results for LGBTQ voters. According to ABC News’ 2026 House voter poll, 87 percent of respondents who identified as gay, lesbian, bisexual or transgender said they voted for a Democratic House candidate, while 12 percent said they voted Republican.

In a New York Post interview, Constantino argued that Democrats “are against the gay community,” and that high-income and hardworking gay voters align better with Republican values around taxes, regulation, border security and gun rights. 

Newsweek has contacted Constantino’s campaign for comment via email outside regular office hours.

Constantino is set to take office in January after narrowly defeating Democrat Blake Gendebien in the 21st Congressional District, a large, mostly rural area in northern and central New York.

The 44-year-old founder of the printing company Sticker Mule and supporter of President Donald Trump faces early friction from local GOP officials, such as Plattsburgh Republican Chair David J. Souliere IV, who urged him to focus on local affordability and health care rather than online rhetoric.

What Constantino Says He Wants to Change

Constantino’s post sets out an initial argument for why gay Americans should support Republicans: a list of priorities that includes taxes, regulation, border security and gun rights.

He has not yet described a campaign or outreach plan, or explained how he would address policy questions that have historically shaped LGBTQ voters’ views of the parties.

How LGBTQ Americans Have Voted

Recent voting data shows the challenge Constantino faces as he works to recruit gay voters to his party. In 2024, NBC’s national exit poll found that 86 percent of LGBTQ voters backed the Democratic candidate, then-Vice President Kamala Harris, while 12 percent backed Trump. 

Exit polling has also shown movement between elections. The same polling series found that Democrat Joe Biden received 64 percent of the LGBTQ vote in 2020, compared with 27 percent for Trump. Those figures describe LGBTQ voters as a group, not gay men alone, and exit polls are estimates rather than a count of every voter.

Survey data on party identity point in a similar direction. A Pew Research Center survey conducted in January 2025 found that 80 percent of LGBTQ adults identified with or leaned toward the Democratic Party, compared with 16 percent who identified with or leaned Republican. The survey was conducted before Trump issued several executive orders related to transgender rights at the beginning of his second term.

Pew also found differences among LGBTQ Republicans and Democrats in how they viewed the parties’ approach to the community. Twenty-four percent of LGBTQ Republicans said the Republican Party was friendly toward gay, lesbian or bisexual people, while 63 percent of LGBTQ Democrats said the same of the Democratic Party. Those views were less favorable when respondents were asked about transgender people.

The Republican Party’s LGBTQ Outreach

Constantino’s pitch also lands amid debate within the Republican Party about its relationship with LGBTQ voters. Log Cabin Republicans is a national organization that promotes Republican candidates and policies to LGBTQ voters. In an August essay, the group’s president, Ross Hemminger, said the organization would refocus its advocacy on lesbian, gay and bisexual issues, ending its advocacy for trans rights.

Republicans have spent years passing bills that target transgender Americans, pushing to roll back marriage equality, and turning our lives into campaign attack ads. You don't get to light the fire and then sell us the extinguisher. "The data isn't close. LGBTQ voters backed Democrats by 86 percent in this month's exit polls. That isn't blind party loyalty. It's a reaction to what Republicans have actually done. If Republicans truly want to earn gay votes, the path is simple. Stop legislating against trans people. Put marriage equality protections into law and keep them there. Support the Equality Act. Protect funding for HIV prevention and care. Until that happens, no post from a congressman-elect is going to change the math." Comeau's 86 percent figure matches reported 2024 presidential exit-poll results for LGBTQ voters. According to ABC News' 2026 House voter poll, 87 percent of respondents who identified as gay, lesbian, bisexual or transgender said they voted for a Democratic House candidate, while 12 percent said they voted Republican. In a New York Post interview, Constantino argued that Democrats "are against the gay community," and that high-income and hardworking gay voters align better with Republican values around taxes, regulation, border security and gun rights. Newsweek has contacted Constantino's campaign for comment via email outside regular office hours. Constantino is set to take office in January after narrowly defeating Democrat Blake Gendebien in the 21st Congressional District, a large, mostly rural area in northern and central New York. The 44-year-old founder of the printing company Sticker Mule and supporter of President Donald Trump faces early friction from local GOP officials, such as Plattsburgh Republican Chair David J. Souliere IV, who urged him to focus on local affordability and health care rather than online rhetoric. What Constantino Says He Wants to Change Constantino's post sets out an initial argument for why gay Americans should support Republicans: a list of priorities that includes taxes, regulation, border security and gun rights. He has not yet described a campaign or outreach plan, or explained how he would address policy questions that have historically shaped LGBTQ voters' views of the parties. How LGBTQ Americans Have Voted Recent voting data shows the challenge Constantino faces as he works to recruit gay voters to his party. In 2024, NBC's national exit poll found that 86 percent of LGBTQ voters backed the Democratic candidate, then-Vice President Kamala Harris, while 12 percent backed Trump. Exit polling has also shown movement between elections. The same polling series found that Democrat Joe Biden received 64 percent of the LGBTQ vote in 2020, compared with 27 percent for Trump. Those figures describe LGBTQ voters as a group, not gay men alone, and exit polls are estimates rather than a count of every voter. Survey data on party identity point in a similar direction. A Pew Research Center survey conducted in January 2025 found that 80 percent of LGBTQ adults identified with or leaned toward the Democratic Party, compared with 16 percent who identified with or leaned Republican. The survey was conducted before Trump issued several executive orders related to transgender rights at the beginning of his second term. Pew also found differences among LGBTQ Republicans and Democrats in how they viewed the parties' approach to the community. Twenty-four percent of LGBTQ Republicans said the Republican Party was friendly toward gay, lesbian or bisexual people, while 63 percent of LGBTQ Democrats said the same of the Democratic Party. Those views were less favorable when respondents were asked about transgender people. The Republican Party’s LGBTQ Outreach Constantino's pitch also lands amid debate within the Republican Party about its relationship with LGBTQ voters. Log Cabin Republicans is a national organization that promotes Republican candidates and policies to LGBTQ voters. In an August essay, the group's president, Ross Hemminger, said the organization would refocus its advocacy on lesbian, gay and bisexual issues, ending its advocacy for trans rights. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Ben Kelly and Shakeema Edwards.
news.summary: Anthony Constantino wants gay Americans in the GOP, though LGBTQ voters have favored Democrats.

The point is not that this movie is better than that movie, but to observe that in the past, a hit movie could have a bigger cultural impact because it permeated a wider swath and a greater proportion of the total population.

That is probably the right outcome. In the wake of his departure, it was already clear that the board had acted too hastily. For all the allegations thrown around, it was far from clear that Huang was really guilty of anything other than breaking his marriage vows. It was not proved that his Chinese mistress, Alice Huang (no relation), was really a “honeypot agent” of the Chinese government, while the second affair, this one with a senior Nvidia executive, may have broken company rules, but was completely consensual. Huang may have acted foolishly. But he had also built Nvidia from nothing and turned it into the world’s largest company, as well as the driving force behind America’s huge global lead in AI. Given that none of the other potential candidates, either internal or external, had anything like the same level of knowledge or ability, bringing him back was the only realistic option. In the wake of the CEO’s return, two points are now clear. To start with, Huang will be more powerful than ever. He may only own 4 percent of the stock, but he has just proved how completely indispensable he is to its future. The Nvidians who didn’t sign the “Stand With Jensen” petition must be feeling, to put it mildly, a little uncomfortable by now, while the position of the board, after making such a mess of the whole process, is surely untenable. The chairman Harvey C. Jones will have to be replaced, and so will most of the other non-executives. Within the company, Huang’s authority will be total. 

And, more importantly, his restoration is a victory for visionary leaders over the dead hand of a few box-ticking, DEI-obsessed corporate functionaries. In reality, leaders of Huang’s fierce intelligence, drive and ambition, are all too rare. In global business, only Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos, Mark Zuckerberg and possibly Anthropic’s Dario Amodei come anywhere close to his level of ability. You can’t change the world by committee, nor can you build a whole new world-changing industry while obsessing over whether all the HR guidelines have been followed. Corporate America has been dialing down the fixation on DEI and political correctness over the last two years. But Huang’s victory over the Nvidia board will confirm it.
