news.title: MAGA II: Con Heir — The War to Inherit Trump’s Republican Revolution
news.text:
“Every great cause begins as a movement, becomes a business, and eventually degenerates into a racket.” —Eric Hoffer, The Temper of Our Time

Remember 2024? Ah, good times: Ben Shapiro was high-fiving Tucker Carlson, Joe Rogan happily endorsed Donald Trump, Elon Musk was proudly “dark MAGA,” and populists, conservatives, libertarians, Evangelists, Tech Bros, Latino men, and Zoomers all hopped aboard the Trump Train. From Mark Levin through RFK Jr. and even the snake-trail to Candace Owens, the MAGA coalition was exceptionally diverse — and ideologically, something of a Rorschach test: Shapiro, Carlson, Rogan, Levin, RFK Jr. and Owens all represented different blocs, and they all expected different policies.

Conflict was inevitable.

And in 2026, someone in MAGA was dating Yoko, ‘cause our band finally broke up. Badly! The same MAGA coalition that propelled the Republican Party to a landslide victory just two years earlier was at war with itself.

Meanwhile, the Democrats were so unified that Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) and the DNC establishment worked hand-in-glove with DSA revolutionaries. (Ain’t it amazing what a common enemy can do to unify a party?)

Other than the two-minutes-to-midnight defection of Haley Stevens, a party so infamously dysfunctional that Will Rogers’ 1920s quip — “I am not a member of any organized political party. I am a Democrat.” — has proven remarkably durable: For nearly a century (!), the Democrats have rarely missed an opportunity to miss an opportunity. They’re the gang that can’t shoot straight.

But not in 2026. The triple-whammy of historic headwinds, five Republican mistakes, and uncommon Democratic unity has fractured the 2024 MAGA coalition beyond repair.

Sorry, but thems the facts: 2024 MAGA is dead, bruh. Shapiro and Carlson aren’t high-fiving anymore — they’re tearing each other apart. Rogan’s support of James Talarico helped mainstream his candidacy. 2024 was fun, but 2026 is a brand-new world — and 2028, we can safely assume, will be even more so.

Okay, then what’s next?

A pair of forces will remake our movement between now and Election Day ’28. The first is President Donald Trump.

Don’t sleep on The Donald: He’s still the most powerful man in the GOP. More than anyone else, his decisions will terraform the 2028 environment. If his popularity rebounds, he’ll have a free hand to grease the wheels for his chosen successor. (And if his popularity fully rebounds, he’ll also be able to co-write the MAGA II platform.)

But if it doesn’t, the next GOP nominee will be chosen — at least, in part — as a rebuke to Trump. Not because we’re traitors, but because electability will be prioritized, and if Trump is an albatross, then separation will be a political necessity.

Which gives us two possible paths: A Trump-lite version of MAGA II, where proximity to Trump is a political asset, or a Trump-free version of MAGA II, where distance from the president is absolutely critical.

The first path is pocket aces for cabinet members like JD Vance and Marco Rubio. The second path is manna from heaven for ex-governors like Ron DeSantis and Glenn Youngkin.

This yuuuuugely matters, because the second force that shapes MAGA II will be the 2028 presidential nominee.

Especially if he wins, because JFK was wrong: Defeat isn’t an orphan — it’s an abortion. Losers don’t have a legacy. Kamala Harris, Mitt Romney, and John Kerry didn’t reshape anything, because they all lost.

Other than mission-focused “lost cause” campaigns like Barry Goldwater and Bernie Sanders, you’ve gotta win to earn a legacy!

So, if Vance snags the ’28 nomination, assembles a losing coalition, and gets blasted by AOC (or whoever), that’s it for the veep. He’ll be a 44-year-old political has-been — a younger, hairier version of Harris.

And that’ll be it for his New Right coalition, too. His proof-of-concept failed, so Republicans will search for a more promising long-term solution. 

Onward Christian soldier.

Vance is stuck: He needs President Trump’s popularity to rebound to win the nomination, but if it rebounds too much, the president will also have veto power over his campaign and platform. (Which will frustrate the hell out of the Carlson bloc.) The veep’s best outcome would be Trump’s popularity rebounding — but (knock on wood) not rebounding too much. That way he’s not an albatross, but he’s also too weak to make policy demands.

Trouble is, that’s also the best outcome for Rubio. And if 2028 prioritizes electability, Rubio will have the upper hand.

(Pro Tip: Thanksgiving week makes perfect PR sense for the secretary of state to time his resignation. Keep your eyes open, because if Rubio doesn’t resign this week, his next-best PR window is Christmas through New Year.)

If the second path emerges, candidates like DeSantis and Youngkin will highlight their anti-Trump credentials. They’d probably pivot to conservatism as their casus belli, making it the intellectual backbone of their MAGA II movement. (Plus, I assume, anti-corruption: With all the Dem investigations, corruption will likely be an ongoing storyline, too.)

Should this happen, we can predict the composition of MAGA II: Whereas MAGA I was more attitudinal, MAGA II will be more ideological.

Furthermore, whereas Trump campaigned as a dealmaking CEO, both DeSantis and Youngkin are ex-governors with legislative experience. They’d likely prioritize effective, predictable governance over transactional wheeling-and-dealing.

It won’t be easy, but if they can cherry-pick enough conservative, libertarian, and culture war policy issues, they could turn MAGA II into something less populist — and more nerdy/wonky.

Which would have two big benefits:

Most political movements are Gail Wynand-like: Instead of being led by a leader, a leader has carefully positioned himself to walk a few steps in front of the movement. 

He’s a LINO: a leader in name only.

One of the things that made MAGA I so special was that it was the exception to the Wynand Rule. Through the sheer force of his personality, Donald Trump and MAGA were one and the same. This was his movement; he owned MAGA, led MAGA, and decided what the hell MAGA meant. Like he said, “MAGA is me.”

There’s no one on the political horizon with a Trump-level personality. Even if Vance, Rubio, DeSantis, Youngkin, or [fill in the blank] wanted to, they lack the chops to win a personality-driven presidential campaign. It’s not in their toolkit.

Which is yet another reason why ideology will make a GOP comeback: Attitude and personal charisma won’t be enough.

Men like Trump are rare. There won’t be a “next Trump” for a very, very long time.

As for which Republican ideas will ultimately prevail, much will depend on the nominee. A Vance victory, for example, would look very different than a Rubio or DeSantis victory.

But we can figure out a few elements: The next nominee will be a pro-life Christian with socially conservative, anti-woke beliefs. None of ‘em are gonna support transitioning children or letting biological boys into girls’ locker rooms. If those are your pet issues, congratulations: You’ll have a home in MAGA II.

Tariffs, trade, AI, taxes, Israel, isolationism, Iran, Ukraine, Canada, NATO, and more, however, are all up for grabs.

And so will immigration. With a Republican in the White House and Democrats in Congress, comprehensive immigration reform is exceedingly unlikely. Which means that media and/or establishment pressure will build for an amnesty-adjacent “compromise.”

Trust me: A number of Republicans will take the bait — because they always do.

The Republican number will grow if President Trump’s influence and popularity weaken. (And if, God forbid, President Trump actually signs a compromise, the backlash from the base would be off-the-charts.)

All in all, it sets the stage for a hellacious 2028. Because SOMEONE will lead MAGA II, whether it’s a Wynand-like leader or the genuine article. And whatever MAGA II ultimately is, it’ll be dramatically different than MAGA I.

Because Eric Hoffer was right: MAGA was a generationally great cause. Which then blossomed into a sprawling, successful ecosystem. And finally, with charlatans like Carlson, Megyn Kelly, and Owens, it degenerated into a racket.

Let’s have a holiday toast: We had a helluva run, boys and girls. We changed the world — and we ain’t done yet. Happy Thanksgiving to you and your family. Cheers!

But after Thanksgiving, our fight continues, so grab a weapon — or we just might find ourselves kicked out of the next great movement.

One Last Thing: We lost the midterms, but our fight continues. Our fight ALWAYS continues. And in many ways, our real fight is just beginning: The radical left has never been so emboldened — or their goals so ambitious.

news.title: Americans Rank Best Recent Presidents: Obama Compared to Trump
news.text: Barack Obama is Americans' choice for the best president of the past 25 years, and Donald Trump is the one they most often rank last, according to a new Politico poll. The Politico Poll asked 2,000 adults to put the four men who have held the White House since 2001 in order from best to worst. Obama came first for 51 percent. Trump was a distant second at 28 percent, followed by George W. Bush at 16 percent and Joe Biden at 5 percent. Trump also landed at the bottom of 52 percent of the rankings. Obama was last for only 8 percent. Pollsters fielded the survey online from November 7 to 10, days after Democrats won both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections. The margin of error is plus or minus 2 percentage points. Obama has led a string of recent polls on presidential popularity, nearly 10 years after leaving office. Trump keeps turning up at both ends of these lists. In a YouGov survey this summer, Americans named him the worst figure in U.S. history even as Republicans picked him as the greatest. Obama vs. Trump The gap between the 44th and 47th presidents has a lot to do with how evenly people judge them. Obama's support runs through the whole list. Besides the 51 percent who put him first, 18 percent ranked him second and 24 percent third. Trump's numbers have almost no middle: 28 percent first, 11 percent second, 9 percent third and a majority last. Obama also pulls some support out of Trump's own coalition. Sixteen percent of Americans who voted for Trump in 2024 ranked Obama as the best of the four, according to the poll. Among Trump voters who don't identify as MAGA, the figure was 23 percent. Other surveys this fall found much the same. An AtlasIntel poll released November 1 showed 54 percent of Americans with a positive image of Obama, compared with 40 percent each for Trump and Biden. In a UMass Lowell/YouGov poll of likely voters in early October, 57 percent viewed Obama favorably. Costas Panagopoulos, a political science professor at Northeastern University, looked at those numbers as both men went out on the midterm trail. "The overall findings are clear: Obama is way better positioned than Trump to be on the campaign trail," he told Newsweek in October. He also pointed out that "retrospective approval of former presidents tends to be higher." Trump has his own ranking. In August he posted a tier list of presidents on Truth Social that put Obama and Biden among the "failures." Inside the Parties: Bush Over Biden For Democrats, the harshest number in the poll belongs to their most recent president. Biden got 5 percent of first-place votes, fewer than any of the others, and 34 percent of adults ranked him last. Moderate Democrats show the problem most clearly. Seventy-six percent of them chose Obama as the best of the four. Bush, at 12 percent, drew more first-place votes from this group than Biden did, and most moderates parked Biden in the middle, with 46 percent ranking him second and 38 percent third. Progressives were kinder to him. Obama was first for 83 percent of progressive Democrats and Biden second for 63 percent. Bush mostly landed third with them, at 62 percent. Party lines decide the bottom of the list. Eighty-eight percent of progressive Democrats and 82 percent of moderates ranked Trump last. Trump voters saved fourth place for Biden: 70 percent of MAGA voters and 61 percent of non-MAGA voters put him there. Only 17 percent of MAGA voters ranked Obama last. Biden "certainly did not leave the presidency in great standing with many Americans," Todd Belt, director of the political management program at George Washington University, told Newsweek. Belt added that many Democrats blamed Biden for Kamala Harris' loss because he did not get out of the race in time. Panagopoulos described a softer landing inside the party. "He has now transitioned into an elder statesman type of role for the Democratic Party," he said in May. "At the end of the day, he is still a former president who remains popular within segments of the Democratic Party." Bush sits in the comfortable middle. Sixteen percent of adults ranked him first, 40 percent second and 38 percent third. Just 7 percent put him last, the smallest share of the four. He left office deeply unpopular amid the Iraq War and the financial crisis. A CNN/SSRS poll in June found 42 percent of Americans now view him favorably and 33 percent unfavorably. Trump's Base Splits MAGA Trump voters are close to unanimous. Eighty-one percent ranked Trump first and 65 percent placed Bush second. The rest of Trump's 2024 coalition is harder to read. Among his voters who don't call themselves MAGA, 42 percent ranked Trump first, 32 percent picked Bush and 23 percent chose Obama. Nineteen percent of them put Trump last. Other polls back up that loyalty. Republicans named Trump their most admired president ahead of Ronald Reagan and Abraham Lincoln, and an Elon University survey found 29 percent of Republicans called him the best president in U.S. history. The same Politico Poll asked Americans which party they expect to win the White House in 2028. Fifty-two percent said Democrats. Among 2024 Trump voters, 22 percent said Democrats would win, while 60 percent expected a Republican and 18 percent were unsure. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Jason Lemon and Trevor Davies
news.summary: Obama tops a new Politico poll ranking the last four presidents, while Trump is most often ranked worst and Biden trails Bush.

news.title: DNC Sets 12 Presidential Primary Debates, Requires Candidates to Denounce ‘Dark Money’
news.text:
The Democratic National Committee (DNC) on Nov. 23 announced 12 debates for the 2028 presidential primary. It also revealed that to qualify, candidates must sign a pledge committing to denouncing outside spending in the selection contest.

The DNC said five debates will be held in 2027 and seven in 2028. The first two are set for June and July 2027, and the final debate is planned for March 2028. The party said it will announce dates, locations, media partners, and qualifying criteria for the first two debates in January.

Debates in the early-voting states will all take place in 2028. Under the calendar that the full DNC approved in August, South Carolina votes first on Jan. 22, 2028, followed by Nevada, New Hampshire, New Mexico, Michigan, and Virginia.

DNC Chairman Ken Martin said the process would keep the party united and strengthen its eventual nominee.

“Democrats are on offense after our historic victories in the midterms, and the DNC is keeping our foot on the gas as we head into the 2028 cycle,” Martin said in a statement.

The DNC said candidates will qualify through polling and other measures of support, such as grassroots fundraising, similar to the 2020 process.

If the field is large, early debates may be split over two consecutive nights, and candidates will be assigned to a night at random. Participation will be capped at 20 candidates across both nights.

To qualify, candidates must also sign the DNC’s Fair Campaign Practices Pledge related to “dark money.” Dark Money refers to “spending meant to influence political outcomes where the source of the money is not disclosed,” according to fundraising tracker OpenSecrets.

The pledge covers ads that a super PAC or a 501(c)(4) group runs on TV, radio, digital platforms, billboards, or mail promoting a candidate or attacking a Democratic opponent. If another primary campaign reports that spending to the DNC and the party notifies the candidate, the candidate must denounce it.

A candidate who fails to do so by the debate qualification deadline is barred from that event and every one after it until the candidate denounces the spending. The DNC says denunciations will be made on a standard statement the party provides to each campaign, and it does not apply to the general election.

Candidates must also agree not to enter joint fundraising agreements with any Democratic Party committee. They also may not request or approve party committee ads at a state, county, or local level that promote them or attack an opponent until a presumptive nominee emerges.

The DNC cited the importance of party neutrality during the nominating process. Under the pledge, a campaign that accepted authorized party spending must refund it, and a prohibited fundraising agreement must be ended and its contributions refunded.

Progressive lawmakers backed the pledge and said it should go further. In a joint statement the DNC released, Reps. Greg Casar (D-Texas), Maxwell Frost (D-Fla.), and Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.), co-chairs of the Congressional Progressive Caucus PAC, called the pledge a first step and said Congress must ban all super PACs by law.

“We urge all 2028 candidates to take this pledge and reject dark money,” they said.

Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) congratulated Martin and said the same approach should be expanded to Senate and House races. Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) said she hoped candidates would not just take the pledge but embrace it.

Candidates may appear at town halls and forums one at a time. A candidate who joins an event where two or more candidates share a stage and answer questions—in person or virtually—will be barred from future DNC debates.

Candidates also can’t campaign in a state that holds an early contest without the party’s approval. Those who do will lose any delegates they win in the early states and be barred from the debates. They must also denounce anyone campaigning for them there.

Which states vote first has been a fight in recent cycles. Iowa led off the Democratic race from 1972 until 2024, when the DNC moved South Carolina to the front at then-President Joe Biden’s request. The party had started rethinking the order after Iowa’s 2020 caucus results were delayed for days.

New Hampshire, whose state law requires it to hold the first primary, went ahead of South Carolina in 2024 anyway. The DNC threatened to strip its convention delegates but restored them after the state party held a second, party-run primary. Rules the party adopted in June bar it from easing penalties after the fact. For 2028, New Hampshire is scheduled third.

The party said it will try to maximize viewership, including by bringing creators and influencers into the debate process.

The DNC’s debate planning committee is led by Minyon Moore, the party’s senior adviser for debates, and Roger Lau, its executive director. Its members include former advisers and staff from the 2020 campaigns of Biden, Sanders, Warren, and Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.).

It also includes alumni from the campaigns of former President Barack Obama, former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, and former Vice President Kamala Harris.

Moore said she is committed to a fair, transparent process that also sets up the nominee to win the general election.
news.summary: Candidates must sign a pledge to denounce super PAC ads and stay out of unsanctioned debates to qualify for the stage, starting in June 2027.

The DNC says denunciations will be made on a standard statement the party provides to each campaign, and it does not apply to the general election.

Candidates must also agree not to enter joint fundraising agreements with any Democratic Party committee. They also may not request or approve party committee ads at a state, county, or local level that promote them or attack an opponent until a presumptive nominee emerges.

The DNC cited the importance of party neutrality during the nominating process. Under the pledge, a campaign that accepted authorized party spending must refund it, and a prohibited fundraising agreement must be ended and its contributions refunded.

Progressive lawmakers backed the pledge and said it should go further. In a joint statement the DNC released, Reps. Greg Casar (D-Texas), Maxwell Frost (D-Fla.), and Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.), co-chairs of the Congressional Progressive Caucus PAC, called the pledge a first step and said Congress must ban all super PACs by law.

“We urge all 2028 candidates to take this pledge and reject dark money,” they said.

Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) congratulated Martin and said the same approach should be expanded to Senate and House races. Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) said she hoped candidates would not just take the pledge but embrace it.

Candidates may appear at town halls and forums one at a time. A candidate who joins an event where two or more candidates share a stage and answer questions—in person or virtually—will be barred from future DNC debates.

Candidates also can’t campaign in a state that holds an early contest without the party’s approval. Those who do will lose any delegates they win in the early states and be barred from the debates. They must also denounce anyone campaigning for them there.

Which states vote first has been a fight in recent cycles. Iowa led off the Democratic race from 1972 until 2024, when the DNC moved South Carolina to the front at then-President Joe Biden’s request. The party had started rethinking the order after Iowa’s 2020 caucus results were delayed for days.

New Hampshire, whose state law requires it to hold the first primary, went ahead of South Carolina in 2024 anyway. The DNC threatened to strip its convention delegates but restored them after the state party held a second, party-run primary. Rules the party adopted in June bar it from easing penalties after the fact. For 2028, New Hampshire is scheduled third.

The party said it will try to maximize viewership, including by bringing creators and influencers into the debate process.

The DNC’s debate planning committee is led by Minyon Moore, the party’s senior adviser for debates, and Roger Lau, its executive director. Its members include former advisers and staff from the 2020 campaigns of Biden, Sanders, Warren, and Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.).

It also includes alumni from the campaigns of former President Barack Obama, former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, and former Vice President Kamala Harris.

Moore said she is committed to a fair, transparent process that also sets up the nominee to win the general election.

news.title: Democrats announce 12 debates starting in June for 2028 race
news.text: The Democratic National Committee on Monday unveiled a debate plan that includes 12 debates starting in June 2027 and running through early 2028 as the field will narrow from what is now a wide-open race.There are still no declared Democratic candidates, although several prominent Democrats have declared interest as the behind-the-scenes primary season has been heating up. DNC chair Ken Martin said the number of participants in the debates will be capped at 20, and the party said if a large number of candidates qualify for a debate, it will be split up over two nights with candidates chosen for each night at random. Martin said the exact dates, media partners and polling and fundraising thresholds would be announced later. Monday's announcement said there will be five debates in 2027 and seven in 2028. In announcing the debate framework, Martin leaned heavily into one of his signature causes, ending dark money in politics. Candidates are required to sign a pledge to publicly denounce super PAC and dark money flowing into their campaigns, although given federal rules around fundraising, it's unclear how the DNC could enforce this rule. The debate schedule comes as Democrats are emboldened by big wins in the midterm elections this month. On Sunday, Democrats secured their 258th seat in the House, giving the party its largest majority since 1992. Democrats won 56 seats in the Senate, including wins in red states like Mississippi, Iowa and South Carolina, which is set to hold the first Democratic primary in 2028. The DNC also held 12 debates starting in June in 2020, the last time the party had a competitive primary. The new plan follows the DNC's decision to change the primary calendar, putting South Carolina first and pushing Iowa's decisive caucuses out of the early window. The DNC says candidates who benefit from certain advertising expenditures by super PACs and "dark money" nonprofits would be required to publicly denounce that support, though the party acknowledges it cannot prohibit such outside spending. The framework also establishes a complaint and review process through which campaigns can raise alleged violations ahead of debate qualification periods.While the pledge requires candidates to publicly denounce super PAC and dark money spending in support of their campaigns, the potentially more consequential change is new restrictions on coordination between campaigns and Democratic Party organizations. The neutrality provisions highlight the party's desire to avoid accusations of favoritism that have dogged Democratic primaries since the 2016 cycle, when critics argued party officials tilted the playing field toward former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton over Sen. Bernie Sanders. And in 2024, former President Joe Biden faced no serious primary challengers and easily clinched the nomination, only to drop out in July after a disastrous debate performance. The party then coalesced behind former Vice President Kamala Harris, despite the concerns of some influential Democrats, who believed an open, albeit truncated, nominating process would be better. The neutrality provisions also build on a longer-running debate among Democrats over the role of outside money in presidential campaigns. During the 2020 primary, Sanders and Sen. Elizabeth Warren made opposition to super PAC and dark-money spending major themes of their campaigns, helping turn outside spending into a litmus test for candidates. Under the 2028 framework, presidential campaigns would be barred from entering into joint fundraising agreements with Democratic Party committees during the primary and could not authorize coordinated spending by state or local Democratic parties on their behalf. Candidates would also be required to sign the pledge and comply with DNC rules governing debate participation.DNC officials say the changes are intended to limit the influence of dark money and maintain party neutrality during a competitive primary. But because the rules do not prevent outside groups from spending on behalf of candidates, the realistic effect is likely to be greater scrutiny of those expenditures rather than a reduction of the amount of outside money flowing into the race. The DNC said that its effort to limit the role of dark money in the primary has received support from progressives including Reps. Greg Casar and Jason Crow, Sens. Andy Kim, Sanders and Warren and former DNC Chair Jaime Harrison.Still, the new rules stop well short of preventing outside groups from participating in the primary. Candidates are only required to disavow a super PAC or nonprofit once, even if that group's spending continues. And because campaigns can file complaints against rivals ahead of debate qualification periods, disputes over compliance could become a recurring feature of the debate process.
news.summary: In announcing the debate framework, DNC chair Ken Martin leaned heavily into one of his signature causes, ending dark money in politics.

news.text:
Greetings, and welcome to Monday, Nov. 23, 2026. It's Thanksgiving week, so the turkey should be thawing in the fridge by now. If it's still rock solid in the freezer, you have a decision to make, and Plan B probably involves a takeout menu. Chinese, maybe?

After 33 years, John Yoo is leaving Berkeley. That takes the number of conservatives teaching constitutional law and history there from one to zero. Berkeley didn't run him off. It didn't have to. It spent decades turning the place into a terrarium where nothing to the right of Elizabeth Warren can survive. And the same rot that cleared dissenters out of the faculty lounge filled the admissions office with racial math and the law school quad with antisemites.

The Korean-born Yoo, the former Bush Justice Department lawyer whom the student paper still dutifully tags as the author of the "torture memos" (Berkeley's version of a scarlet letter), described the problem in a New York Post column reasonably well:

They are sacrificing the cultivation of excellent students and scholars of diverse views to increase the numbers of those with the superficial characteristics of skin color and gender.That's left them vulnerable to virulent ideologies like antisemitism and anti-Western Marxism.

That's the whole indictment in two sentences. Now let's walk the evidence into court, which is more than Berkeley's student groups would let a conservative do.

The hiring hall

Yoo writes that Berkeley "has consistently rejected conservative scholars," no matter how qualified, well-published, or widely cited. In his farewell email to colleagues, he joked that his exit would cut the number of conservative public-law professors at Berkeley by 100 percent. In the Post, he noted that Berkeley students "used to be good at math." Hold that thought. We'll come back to it.

Berkeley says the quiet part out loud in the faculty lounge, just never on paper. Yoo recounts a famous professor in one of Berkeley's top-ranked humanities departments telling him flatly that he would never hire a conservative. His reasoning: conservatives defend hierarchy, and real scholars question it. Apparently it never occurred to the good professor that on a modern campus, he is the hierarchy, and the only people questioning it are the ones he refuses to hire. That's not scholarship. That's a bouncer with tenure. Until, of course, the Birkenstock-wearing crowd comes for him. 

Meanwhile, according to Yoo, hiring committees favor candidates by race, ethnicity, and sex, while taking care never to leave a paper trail, because California law forbids it. Nothing says "we're proud of this policy" quite like shredding the evidence. The Justice Department evidently got curious too. It opened an investigation into race- and sex-based employment discrimination across the UC system.

The result is the monoculture you'd expect. A voter-registration study of 23 Berkeley departments found 9.9 registered Democrats for every Republican. That was 20 years ago, and now that Yoo is gone, nobody can say with a straight face that the ratio has improved. Across 40 leading universities, law faculties run 8.6 to 1, and history departments 33.5 to 1. You'd find more ideological variety at a North Korean party congress, and the snacks would be about as good. Yoo calls Berkeley a place that "wallows contentedly in a monoculture of liberalism." I think he's being overly generous, though for what purpose, I cannot fathom. Maybe he still wants the faculty Christmas card. (Sorry, the "winter solstice" card. I keep forgetting). 

The admissions office

Now, back to that math.

On September 9, the Justice Department and the Department of Education found Berkeley Law in violation of Title VI of the Civil Rights Act in admitting its 2024 and 2025 classes. The case rests on Berkeley Law's own applicant data, which shows that in 2025, black applicants had 5.8 times higher odds of admission than comparable white applicants. Over five years, the median black admit scored around 165 on the LSAT, Hispanic admits about 169, and white and Asian admits about 172. On a test that tops out at 180, that isn't a rounding error. It's a policy with a press office.

California voters banned racial preferences in public education with Proposition 209 back in 1996. The Supreme Court finished the job nationally in Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard in 2023. According to federal investigators, Berkeley got around both with essay prompts and other racial proxies. Applicants write about their identity, and the readers do the rest. It's affirmative action with a fake mustache and a library card. The government's letter accused Dean Erwin Chemerinsky of deliberately trying to circumvent the court's ruling. Chemerinsky insists the school "scrupulously complies" with the law. Every card sharp scrupulously complies until somebody counts the aces.

Undergraduates get the same treatment. Students Against Racial Discrimination has sued the entire UC system, alleging racial preferences at all nine undergraduate campuses.

So Yoo is correct that Berkeley's students used to be good at math. Its administrators still are. They just solve for a different variable, and they show their work only under subpoena and then kicking and screaming about how they were forced into it.

The harvest

Build a campus that sorts people by skin color and refuses to hire anybody who might argue back, and you've built a campus with no immune system. Then Oct. 7, 2023, arrived, and the infection went septic.

Yoo, who survived protesters picketing his classes and tree-sitters camped outside his office (the Left is fiercely pro-life, so long as the life in question is that of a tree), says he'd never seen anything like it. Most student groups at Berkeley Law, he writes, now boycott any speaker who believes Israel has a right to exist. That isn't hyperbole. Student groups at the law school adopted bylaws barring Zionist speakers, and the Brandeis Center eventually counted at least 23 campus organizations with such bans. Future civil-rights lawyers drew up blacklists by religion and nationality and called it activism. Somewhere, a 1950s Southern country club is asking for royalties. And for the first time in his 33 years, Yoo writes, he watched a heckler's veto silence an Israeli lawmaker while top university officials stood around like mall cops at a smash-and-grab.

Then the mob came for the dean himself. Before an April 2024 dinner Chemerinsky hosted at his home for graduating students, activists plastered campus with a flyer showing him clutching a bloody knife and fork under the words "No dinner with Zionist Chem while Gaza starves!" At the dinner, a student leader of Law Students for Justice in Palestine grabbed a microphone and turned his backyard into a protest stage, and refused to leave when asked. Free food, and they still couldn't manage gratitude.

Savor the irony. The dean the feds accuse of gaming admissions in the name of diversity became a target of the very ideology that diversity-first campuses incubate. The revolution always gets around to the guy who set the table. And so the Left eats its own, on ideological grounds, once again. Yoo, who says he rarely agrees with Chemerinsky, rightly calls what happened to him antisemitism. The oppressor-oppressed worldview always puts the Jews in the oppressor column, and it doesn't care how many liberal merit badges a particular Jew has sewn on his sash.

Berkeley didn't clean house on its own. A lawsuit made it. In March, the university settled with the Brandeis Center, agreeing to pay $1 million in legal fees, scrap the anti-Zionist bylaws, and impose mandatory antidiscrimination training. That's the same training regime that produced the problem, now aimed in a new direction. Federal investigators, meanwhile, opened a pattern-or-practice probe into antisemitism across UC, and Berkeley turned over about 160 names tied to antisemitism reports.

Yoo's prescription is at least partly right: put Western civilization back at the center of the curriculum with the list of points provided by Russell Kirk in his 1974 book, The Roots of American Order, which I've often referred to in previous columns. Reason from Athens, revelation from Jerusalem, and the free markets, natural rights, and self-government that grew from both. Teach it, he says, not to worship the past but to understand and argue with it. 

That's part of the antidote to a worldview that hates the very civilization that built the university. The rest is something I've been calling for for years: pry government off the other end of the leash attached to our centers of higher learning. And, no shock, that's the one part of this Yoo doesn't even allude to. I really must wonder why.

Look, does anyone seriously expect a government-run, taxpayer-funded educational system to teach young minds full of mush the virtues of limited government? Especially one that also cashes checks from Beijing? Congress called out Berkeley for failing to properly report more than $200 million in funding from China, and the Trump administration opened its own investigation into Berkeley's foreign funding. Expecting that crowd to teach the principles of a free republic is like hiring the fox to run a poultry-science seminar.

Berkeley's faculty, Yoo says, treats the defense of Western civilization as reactionary at best. Yes. I've been saying the same for 30-some years now, about the entirety of government-run education, and Berkeley wasn't listening then either. So he's taking his act to the University of Texas at Austin's School of Civic Leadership, where the administration actually wants students reading the great books.

Wait. Austin? 

Let's make sure we understand this. Yoo is leaving a deep-blue city for the deepest-blue spot in Texas. In 2024, 68.7% of Travis County voters went for Kamala Harris and 29.4% for Donald Trump, at a time when Harris won just 12 of Texas' 254 counties. "Keep Austin Weird" was never a conservative slogan, and the UT faculty is hardly a Federalist Society chapter. He's traded the San Francisco Bay for Lady Bird Lake. OK, granted, It's a marginally better situation than Berkeley, but a half step at best.

Well, no shock. I've long held that Yoo is at best a centrist, not a conservative. I came to that conclusion back when he was on his perch in the Bush administration. I wrote back then that Yoo tended to ignore the baseline conflicts of logic that position puts him in. So, this half step is right in line with his history.

And notice what makes his new home possible. The School of Civic Leadership exists because Texas politicians funded it over the faculty's grumbling, with the UT System putting $100 million into a building for it. Yoo didn't escape the government leash. He just found a friendlier hand holding it. That works fine right up until the other party grabs the leash. That's a point Yoo apparently hasn't considered. Or perhaps he's actively avoiding it. 

In any event, Berkeley supposedly wanted a faculty and a student body that looked diverse in the brochure. It got exactly what it bargained for in reality: one that thinks in lockstep, games the law it's sworn to obey, and lets antisemites run the student groups at its own law school. Now it has also lost the one man on its public-law faculty willing to say so out loud. As Rush Limbaugh used to say, the only diversity the left can't stand is diversity of thought.

I do have to wonder what Austin will look like 30 years from now. Probably like Berkeley today, assuming big government still holds its leash. My guess is that Yoo, being nearly 60 now, won't be around long enough to move out in 30 years when Austin, being on the arc it's on, becomes too much for him as Berkeley did.

Don’t miss my latest interview on “The Road Forward” with Dr. Tim Clinton, president of the American Association of Christian Counselors. Dr. Clinton and I discuss the string of recent tech outages, the elections and what we should be grateful for this Thanksgiving. Good News 

The Supreme Court overturned a lower court ruling requiring men claiming to be women to be placed in female prisons. This is a victory for common sense. The Third Circuit Court of Appeals rejected an attempt by Rep. LaMonica McIver (D-NJ) to have the charges against her for assaulting a federal immigration police officer dismissed. A federal judge ruled that school boards in Maine discriminated against conservative churches by denying them meeting space in empty schools on weekends based on their traditional beliefs. The ruling is a victory for religious liberty. Texas officials announced that they are launching statewide risk-limiting audits of the U.S. Senate and the race for chief justice of the Texas Supreme Court. news.title: What If We Told You She’s a Mastermind? A Tale of Pop Stardom
news.text:
She has romantic associations with celebrities—some of whom treat her -badly, including a member of a boy band who breaks up with her over a 27-second phone call. By that pOint, she is a celebrity herself. But fame has not warped her the way it has nearly everybody else: She doesn’t even have a manager! What she has are her many great friends. She tells them everything and is pleasantly surprised when they do not put her on blast.
At 29, the record company from Nashville betrays her by selling her life’s work to her archnemesis’s manager. She would have bought the rights to her own songs, only she was never afforded the chance. The sale between the two men occurs without her knowing. When she finds out, she appeals to her loyal fans, who defend her in her moral outrage. With their support, she wins the rights to her music. By then, she’s met her shining knight. After a happy and very public courtship, your English and your gym teachers wed.
When the curtain falls on humanity, they will say that for a time, she defined American sonic life—that her music owned the ’10s and the long ’20s.
B SIDE A child is born and grows up on an 11-acre Christmas tree farm that her third-generation banker father bought from a client at Merrill Lynch, where he is a vice president and manages a portfolio around $270 million. When she is 10 years old, the family moves to a 3,560-square-foot, five-bedroom, three-and-a-half-bath Georgian Colonial in Wyomissing, Pennsylvania. A visitor calls the house a “six-star hotel.”
Her mOther is “definitely a theater mom, very aggressive,” says Sandy Carbone, whose son directs The Star in Grease, Bye Bye Birdie, The Sound of Music. The mom asks Carbone’s other son, a computer repairman named Ronnie Cremer, if he might teach her daughter to play a 12-string guitar. “She used to complain a lot about the guitar chords,” Cremer says, “that it hurt her hands.” Cremer relays this to the parents. “Just keep worKing her,” they reply. “She needs this to get better.”
Once, during a lesson, the mother returns home with Taco Bell. The girl, who is not yet a star, scampers to the kitchen, but salad is her lot. “Nobody wants to see a fat pop star,” Cremer recalls the mother saying. (Cremer first told the New York Daily News this story in 2015. The Star declined to comment then. Vanity Fair sent The Star multiple questions while reporting this story; she declined to comment.)
Her father’s connections lead to his daughter singing the national anthem before a minor league baseball game, which leads to another performance, which he videotapes and sends to a marketing manager for the Philadelphia 76ers. Which is how she ends up singing the national anthem for them, wearing red, white, and blue.
Four months into her guitar-playing career, according to Cremer, her father begins driving his daughter to various gigs, giving away tickets to business associates and other acquaintances. Cremer says her father asks that they cheer his daughter loudly so she always seems to be playing to a full house. He captures these performances on tape to send to Nashville, before moving the family there.
Her fame grows. She becomes a Star. Her erstwhile suitors grouse that the songs she writes about them are misrepresentations—that their relationship lasted only a few weeks, or that the call was 27 seconds because she hung up first. In lieu of a manager, what The Star has is her mother and a closed board of stakeholders. Her many friends do not dare speak ill of her—dare not speak of her at all.
By 2006 the father has a stake in the Nashville record company, after making a financial investment worth a reported $500,000, according to Music Business Worldwide. He makes $15 million when it sells. In 2023 she becomes a billionaire on account of her tour, the highest grossing of all time. Her fans do not mind. “Of all the billionaires,” a fan says, “she is my favorite billionaire!”
When the curtain falls on humanity, they will say that for a time she defined American sonic life—that her music owned the ’10s and the long ’20s.
A SIDE The Star is beloved. -Universally, famously. She is friendship bracelets. She is sold-out stadiums. She is honorary degrees. She is a wedding reception for 1,000 and $26 million to charity for the inconvenience to any. She says vote and tens of thousands register. She wears a bandeau “nap top” and midi skirt, and everyone else buys a bandeau nap top and midi skirt. She is our most gracious homecoming queen, our Miss Americana. In these divided times, everybody agrees: The Star is power.
B SIDE Across her 12 eras and interviews with over 100 people who worked with her, who Work with her, who were her confidants, contemporaries, scholars, critics, other anoraks, nemeses, neighbors, classmates, teachers, and lover, what emerges as The Star’s most enduring identity is not musician, not artist, not celebrity, but a combination of victim and victimizer.
The dissenting chorus has penned its own folklore about how The Star often seems to present herself as persecuted even as she sits on a throne of gold and diamonds. Cold, they say, is the steel of her ax to grind. She may not have explicitly ordered her detractors to be banned from parties and other social occasions, or banned her friends from collaborating with her perceived opponents, but tHe results are just that.
Her highness is controlling and manipulative, they say—of charts, of public opinion, of social dynamics. They say she has been known to crucify those who cross her. Others say The Star weaponizes her sense of victimhood, that by foregrounding her own suffering, she believes she is speaking from a position of superior virtue. “She is punitive,” says a music industry professional we’ll call The Exec. “She loves to smack people in the heAd” figuratively, says a person familiar with the matter who used to be close with The Star. We’ll refer to them as The Person Familiar. “This is her way of feeling like she can discipline people.”
A lawyer with knowledge of The Star declined to be interviewed using their own phone, choosing to speak instead through an intermediary. A manager asked for our correspondence to be deleted. A pasTor from her childhood church said they could not speak without express permission from The Star’s family. When these mortals did speak of The Star in public—in line, at the airport, mid-flight, on foot, on the job, at pickup, on the way to grocery stores, parks, or yoga—it was softly, using initials. A Washington Post reporter who recently wrote a book about The Star has noted that countless sources refused to go on the record even to say nice things about her.
Someone who previouslY collaborated with The Star—and asked that their profession not be mentioned because The Star had worked with so few with this specific job—advised I turn down this assignment. Did they think The Star would read the article, though? “Oh yes.”
The Star’s Manichaean notion of the world means “if you’re in the circle, she takes amazing care of you”—according to a musician who toured with her and spoke from behind the scrim of a nondisclosure agreement.
If you’re not, you face social censure. “If you look at history,” says The Person Familiar, “she’s always had villains. Back to her high school days.” Or earlier.
A SIDE When she was young, The Star told Katie Couric in 2009, she had no friends. Or rather, “I had that group of friends when I was about 12. [Then] they all just decided they didn’t wanna hang out with me anymore. I would go and sit dOwn at the lunch table with my friends. And they would get up and move their trays to another table.” If one definition of artist is “a person uniquely sensitive to the vicissitudes of life, from whence their great art comes; someone for whom much happens, and mUch more is expected in return,” then the original pain of The Star appears to be this early sense of loss: the agony of being passed over or feeling lost among peers. No amount of later validation, it seems, would allay it.
B SIDE “That wasn’t true,” says Sharon Luyben. “We had assigned seating in junior high.” (One former classmate of The Star recalls assigned seating at lunch; another isn’t sure. The Wyomissing Area School District did not respond to questions.)
Luyben—Mrs. Luyben to The Star—had been the music teacher at Wyomissing Area Junior/Senior High for 34 years. She taught The Star in seventh and eighth grades and then again on Sundays at their church. They first met during a 2002 production of The Sound of Music in which The Star played an older von Trapp child. (She played Maria, the lead, in a different production.)
Chanice Skinner, who sat next to The Star in Luyben’s class, recalls The Star being “always part of the popular crowd,” among preppy kids who wore Ralph Lauren shirts with the collars popped. “If you weren’t part of her friend group,” Skinner says, “you didn’t exist to her.” Years later she was watching a Target commercial in which The Star talked about being bullied. “I was like, You were part of that. What are you talking about? If anything, you were one of the bullies.”
In Skinner’s estimation, The Star’s success, like so many aspects of American life, was overdetermined. “That’s what happens when you have a faMily that is already well-off and able to back you, [to] fund your dream.” Did it seem, though, that The Star carried exceptional promise? “We all had promise,” says Skinner, who starred in plays with The Star and now sells industrial saws in West Reading. “It’s just that she had money.”
Arielle Peppers was a year behind The Star and sat on the other side of Skinner in Luyben’s class for multiple quarters. She remembers The Star coming to class in Ugg boots. Peppers had transferred from the nearby city of ReAding after her neighbor was stabbed in the neck. She asked her mother for a pair of the same boots. “Do you know how much they cost?” her mother said. A pair of Uggs amounted to half her single mother’s paycheck working variously at a bakery, at a dairy mill, and as a caretaker. Peppers recalls The Star owning multiples of Uggs: “She had the brown one, the black one, the blue one.”
Peppers, who works as a caretaker while maintaining her music practice (under the stage name A.Star), remembers The Star being teased on a single occasion: at a school talent show, when she sang about her crush on a classmate called Corey. (In the aforementioneD 2010 Target commercial, The Star recalls having a crush on a boy named “Corey Robertson” when she was in fourth grade.) The Star had brought her own sound system to perform a song her classmates remember being about “Corey’s eyes.” The Star’s mother helped set it up. The Star won.
The Star’s debut album, released in 2006, includes a song called “Stay Beautiful” that starts like this: “Cory’s eyes”—spelled without the e—“are like a jungle / He smiles, it’s like the radio.”
A SIDE Every Starbucks lover and their mother—or their manager—knows the story. The Star convinces her parents to move to Nashville so she can try her luck in country music. Her music reportedly finds its way to The Machine—an executive from Nashville—in part through his wife, who gets it through a music executive The Star’s father knows. Fame follows.
In time, The Machine decides to sell the label. He tells The Star of his intention and says that he is willing to part with her master recordings—accounting for 50 to 80 percent of the label’s revenue—only if The Star agrees to makE new music in exchange for old, the same bad deal that stymied musicians like Prince and Janet Jackson. The Star has fought many a battle in her time, a great deal of them against men who mean her harm. It is impossible, she cries, to be a woman in the music industry; history proves her right over and over.
A high-profile Manager representing top talent—some of whom have feuded with The Star, including Justin Bieber—hears the news and calls The Machine. On June 28, 2019, The Machine’s board approves a sale, giving The Manager control of The Star’s masters. Two days later The Star takes to Tumblr.
B SIDE Her kingdom terrorized, The Star rises to defend her doMinion. She takes special umbrage with The Manager, accusing him of “incessant, manipulative bullying.” The Person Familiar alleges The Star only ever spoke fondly of The Manager, while The Manager alleges he met The Star only three times, according to The Free Press.
In her Tumblr post, she also mentions an illegal recording of a phone call between her and an archnemesis. The Person Familiar contends they told The Star at the time it was a bad idea to let the nemesis use her name in a certain famous song. Eventually, it seems The Star would come to agree with them.
The Star’s fans send death threats to The Manager. The Manager relays this to The Star’s team; he does not hear from her. He does hear from others who were allegedly smote by The Star for their perceived treachery. They welcome him into the fellowship of the chastened. Mutual friends of both The Star and The -Manager—a -singer, a talk show host, an actor—try to help them make up to no avail.
Meanwhile, The Star begins rerecording her old albums, depreciating the value of the originals enough to buy them all back eventually. A hitherto unprecedented feat, it is declared a victory for the people. It’s certainly a victory to The Star, who, in making herself a metonym for all womEn, successfully equates criticism against her as criticism against womenkind.
A SIDE Since her debut in 2006, The Star has been celebrated for her very brilliant songwriting—often about the marriage plot or the pains and possibilities of living in the snakeskin of an ended relationship, but also about historical figures, or literary characters, or herself. There are only so many ways to say “Love me” or “Treat me right,” and she says them all, with tremendous emotional fluency. And she does it all in rhyme, that hooked-up sound so pleasing to the human ear. “There is a reason,” poet Michael Robbins says, “we don’t say penis pic. We say dick pic.”
Also: She is generous to fellow musicians, many of whom open for her, then ascend to new heights of fame. Many remain in her orbit.
Years after opening for The Star on tour, another pop star—let’s call her The Brat—releases her sixth studio album, where she explores the vulnerability she feels next to The Star. Despite the jab, in August 2024, The Star tells New York that she has been blown away by The Brat’s “melodic sensibilities,” calling her lyrics “surreal and inventive.” She adds, “I love to see hard work like that pay off.” In February 2025, The Star is seen dancing jubilantly to The Brat as she performs onstage. The Star is benevolent; she rises above.
B SIDE The Star has historically urged her listeners not to separate the art from the artist, openly turning her life into lyrics and lyrics into hits. It is verboten, however, for others to use her as their source material. Only on her watch may one be casually cruel in the name of being honest.
In 2018, after The Brat opened for The Star, The Star began platonically courting The Brat, inviting her into her inner circle. The Brat shied from The Star’s advances—because...brat—even when she and The Star dated men in the same English rock band.
In 2024, The Brat released a song about her insecurities around the world’s biggest pop star: “I couldn’t even be her if I tried,” she sings. “I’m opposite, I’m on the other side.”
In 2025, The Star seemed to clap back to The Brat by releasing a song of her own about their relationship. In it, she accused The Brat of consuming illegal substances—which is fair enough.
In the time since The Brat released a song about The Star, The Exec says, The Star has “done this performance that she’s supportive of her...but she’s not.” In fact, says The Exec, artists who seem earmarked as The Star’s intentionally DO not collaborate professionally with her rivals, who also seem to be barred from taking part in her social world.
The incident recalled other entangle-ments with other brunettes. A Protégé was affiliated with The Star until 2021, when she sent her debut album to the wife of her archnemesis. Seven-ish weeks later, The Protégé credited The Star on a song, which one occasionally does to ward off litigation and fan outcry, according to copyright lawyers.
In 2023, The Protégé released a song that appeared to intimate a falling-out between her and a once-beloved mentor: “Trust that you betrayed, confusion that still lingers / Took everything I loved and crushed it in between your fingers.” But then, at the 2024 Grammys, The Star was seen vibing to The Protégé’s performance.
Before that was The California Girl—an adult pretending to be a child—and her feud with The Star, who might be a child pretending to be an adult. And, of course, the Kardashian affair, the details of which we are excluding from this narrative. (Yet another protégé, let’s call her The Blonde, remains in The Star’s good graces.)
“It’s truly Regina George,” The Exec says.
There once lived a music critic who dared pan The Star. Around then, members of her friend group, one of whom she lived with, were getting courted by The Star. The Critic felt The Star was “ordering friends from a catalog.” After her negative review ran, The Critic’s friends—professional musicians all, who previously credited The Critic for their early success—shunned her. Her roommate, seemingly of her own accord, asked her to move out of their shared duplex. The Star had won.
A SIDE In a 2020 documentary about herself, The Star repeated a story she has often told about how a big part of her feels frozen at 16, when she became famous. Though if she is frozen at 16, she has repeatedly—and mightily—fought against stasis. In her younger years, she avoided electoral politics, could not see how articulating her opinion was necessary. Later, she found her voice, making statements and endorsements for Democratic candidates, including Kamala Harris for president. She speaks in favor of LGBTQ+ rights, gun control, and making Juneteenth a national holiday. She becomes someone on whom nothing is lost.
B SIDE You only become famous if you really, really want to. Lana Del Rey said as much to the BBC in 2024. And The Star really, really did. “She wants it,” Del Rey said. “She’s told me so many times she wants it more than anyone.”
But if fame is a fickle food, as -Emily Dickinson—The Star’s sixth cousin, according to Ancestry.com—observed, it is also impunity. You might end up like Barbra Streisand, cloning Coton de Tulears and building a mall in your basement. Or like Jim Carrey, watching YouTube videos all day from your estate in Maui. Or like whatever Elon Musk is doing right now.
Fame also fractures trust. A life grows and shrinks in inverse proportion to the size of its celebrity.
When they were close, The Person Familiar says, The Star’s professional life was run by a cabinet of three, including her mother, who acts as The Star’s manager; her longtime tour manager; and her publicist, to whom we only beg for mercy.
“Nobody is beyond reproach with her,” says The Person Familiar. Perhaps not even The Star’s sometimes close and dear friend who, after their private correspondence spilled across the tabloids as part of a public lawsuit, was not seen at The Star’s wedding. “If you don’t see it her way, she comes after you.”
“It’s always the same,” The Person Familiar says. “They say something she doesn’t like and they are dead to her. She’d be at dinner at [redacted]’s, then three weeks later, ‘Oh no, I hate her guts.’ ”
A/B SIDE Okay, so The Star has a reputation for being punitive. She seems too invested in her own victimhood. Where might she have learned to be so?
Why, us, of course.
Stars function, as cultural theorist Stuart Hall observed, as a mirror. “I want you to know / I’m a mirrorball,” The Star sang in a 2020 hit. “I’ll show you every version of yourself tonight.”
The Star holds up a mirror to us, and what the mirror says is this: If churches were once our society’s primary source of community, identity, and meaning, in these secular times we turn instead to celebrities. And we look, especially, to singers, because who among us is immune to music? The way a song can pitch you forward in space, sustain you through time; the way you swear some songs are written just for you.
A SIDE Stars, they’re just like us. Despite her life in perfect meter, lasting love had long eluded The Star. But it turned out she was a princess, this was a fairy tale, and we were in Hollywood. Her latest beau—regretfully we must call him Redwood—brought to her life a new form of intensity, a golden light, as they courted at a stadium show, a podcast interview, more shows, in Instagram posts. They have so much in common, The Star points out: They both perform at stadiums. He practices; she rehearses. He plays games, she plays shows.
And all she had ever wanted from the world was that it celebrate her milky goodness, that her altruism not be mistaken for covert narcissism. Ahead of her wedding, the happy couple donates $26 million to local charities. Since then, The Star released four new songs, launched an Oscar campaign, including performing at the Academy Museum Gala, and got a haircut.
B SIDE Summer 2026. The world’s most famous sexy baby—who insists that she is really a monster on a hill—chooses, as the site of her nuptials, midtown Manhattan during a heat wave. Her guests nibble on buffet food as thousands of New Yorkers lose power.
It is not lost on them that her $26 million giveaway, apart from being a tax write-off, is akin to a person making $81,228—the median household income in New York City—giving away $1,055. (In fall 2025, when this article was commissioned, The Star was worth $1.6 billion. By the time this issue goes to press, she will be worth over $2 billion, or the GDP of Eritrea.)
“To become a billionaire,” The Star’s ex Matt Healy once told the Doomscroll podcast, “you don’t really care that much about culture.” He wasn’t speaking specifically about The Star but the deadening effects of modern wealth. Beyond need lies want. Beyond want, greed.
A/B SIDE And beyond greed was a tricked-out walled garden for the enchanted, her betrothed, and 1,000 of their family and friends, including, according to news reports, at least one government contractor who did not respond to multiple requests for comment. (In March his company took over our nation’s largest ICE detention facility. Earlier this year a father of three was pronounced dead there, after struggling with five guards, the second death at the camp in as many months. His name was Geraldo Lunas Campos.)
In other news, the wedding reportedly featured a raffle where a lucky guest won a Chanel bag. Another allegedly won a 1970 Chevrolet Chevelle. Madison Square Garden Entertainment Corp. reportedly locked out its own security staff for the occasion, like it was a Mob bar—the kind with no windows. Not even members of the New York Police Department were allowed their own phones on site.
Love may be free, but the performance of it is not. It requires crates, trucks, officers on overtime, private jets, SUVs, HVACs, all the queen’s horses, all the queen’s men, a Jumbotron. Conspiracy theories do not tell you the truth, but they do tell a kind of psychological truth about a place or its people. Had The Star and Redwood filmed the ceremony, perhaps for theatrical release or streaming—maybe on Disney+, which paid The Star a king’s ransom for the rights to another project? (A person with knowledge says the couple has no plans to drop a documentary about their big day.)
Around the barricades of Madison Square Garden, in the wake left by The Star, her groom, and their guests, her fans gathered. Some had been there for hours, wanting to be nearer to their pious majesty. A white truck passed. Pastries—from the merrymaking gentry presumably, though who can say for certain—were distributed, with an assist from a cop in uniform and gear.
If you listened carefully then to the sounds of the city—not for any semantic meaning, but if you were to really pitch your ears to the utopic promise of music—you might have heard the determined whoosh of a weighted blade dropping, dropping, dropping, the ax of public opinion falling in downward demotic motion.
(The Star’s version was used in the making of this article.)
news.summary: Once upon a time, a country girl became the biggest star on the planet. But after speaking to over 100 sources, May Jeong finds there’s more than one version of this fairy tale.

news.title: DNC sets 12 presidential debates with first dark-money pledge requirement
news.text:
The Democratic National Committee announced Monday it will hold 12 presidential primary debates for 2028, beginning in June 2027, with candidates required to pledge to disavow dark money to qualify.

The party expects a crowded field, and the pledge will be a first for debate qualification, a requirement DNC Chairman Ken Martin has advocated.

The schedule calls for five debates in 2027 and seven in 2028, ending in March 2028. The DNC said it "reserves the right to adjust the schedule as necessary."

"Democrats are on offense after our historic victories in the midterms, and the DNC is keeping our foot on the gas as we head into the 2028 cycle," Martin said.

Rules for outside spending

To reach the stage, candidates must "sign and follow the DNC’s Fair Campaign Practices Pledge committing to denounce dark money spending in our primary in order to qualify for debate participation," the committee said.

Martin brought a proposal to DNC members in August 2025 to examine limits on corporate and dark-money spending in the presidential primary.

Candidates must also disavow any super PACs or dark-money groups that run ads backing them or attacking their opponents, Axios reported. The DNC plans to track those disavowals on its website, along with any complaints alleging that candidates are not following the rules.

The DNC said neither rule covers the 2028 general election or groups attacking Republicans that do not support a particular Democrat.

A DNC official told Axios that progressive senators Bernie Sanders and Elizabeth Warren support the change, as do more moderate Democrats including Representative Jason Crow and former DNC chair Jaime Harrison.

A person close to Martin told Axios the party wants to build on its midterm message opposing dark money and what the person called corruption by Elon Musk and other ultra-wealthy special interests. That message resonated across the ideological spectrum, the person said, while government corruption was a top concern for midterm voters, according to The Associated Press.

Axios said it was unclear whether the change would have a substantive effect or be symbolic, noting that most likely Democratic candidates had been expected to rely on super PACs. The groups cannot legally coordinate directly with candidates, but they can still spend to help candidates who disavow them.

Midterms and the field

Democrats took control of both the House and Senate in this month’s midterms. They have won at least 258 House seats, giving them their largest House majority since 1992, according to an Associated Press tally.

The party has no clear 2028 frontrunner. No major candidate has launched a campaign to succeed Republican President Donald Trump, who is term-limited.

Last week, allies of former Vice President Kamala Harris formed a committee urging her to run, the Los Angeles Times reported. Since the election, committees have also formed to encourage Representatives Ro Khanna and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg to enter the race.

"It does feel like the shadow primary is underway," said Jim Demers, a veteran Democratic strategist in New Hampshire.

Debate qualification

The DNC said its qualifying criteria will resemble those from 2020, when a large field took part in a dozen debates. Candidates will need to meet polling and grassroots fundraising requirements.

If necessary, participation will be limited to 20 qualifying candidates per debate across two nights. The early debates could take place over consecutive nights.

Minyon Moore, the DNC’s senior adviser for debates, and Executive Director Roger Lau will lead the planning committee, whose members include staff and advisers from past Democratic presidential campaigns. Moore said she is committed to a process that "sets our nominee up for success in the general election."

Earlier this year, the DNC reduced its list of potential 2028 convention hosts to Boston, Denver and Philadelphia.

The DNC said it will announce in January 2027 the locations, times and media partners for the first two debates, as well as the precise ways candidates can qualify.
news.summary: The schedule starts in June 2027, and candidates must pledge to denounce dark money spending to qualify.

news.title: 'Liberal psyops' aren't enough to beat the right-wing media machine
news.text:
The president fell asleep again. He was listening to a speech by Xi Jinping, the head of the Chinese Communist Party. Seated, with hands clasped, Donald Trump’s eyes closed and stayed closed. The moment was played on a giant screen at the APEC summit’s media center. Reporters laughed. They took pictures. It was big news everywhere, except in America.

Here it was just more of the same. Why? 

The Bulwark's Sarah Longwell has a theory: “One weird trick that Trump and his inner circle have been able to pull off is taking a Democratic scandal — Hillary’s server, Hunter’s laptop, sleepy Joe — and committing the same offense — security lapses, monetizing access, literally falling asleep — by putting rocket fuel under them to achieve enormous scale. Somehow by being 1,000 times scale of magnitude worse than the Democratic scandal, they overwhelm the system. The scandals are too big for the discourse to really get its arms around.”

That’s not quite right, though. Fox and other cable networks, Twitter, Meta, TikTok – and increasingly CBS News, CNN and other legacy outlets – these are, in various ways, part of the rightwing media apparatus. Scandals involving Trump rarely break through, not because the discourse can’t get its arms around them, but because the discourse makes them so normal as to be invisible. Old age was a scandal for Joe Biden. It was existential crisis for his party. 

For Trump, it’s Tuesday.

Our media environment is now so slanted to the right that Americans often know less about what the Democrats say than about what the Republicans say the Democrats say, a dynamic that greatly determined the outcome of the 2024 election. Acknowledging this reality, some on the left have overcome their natural disgust for propaganda in order to call for a left-coded media environment of their own. In response, the Democratic National Committee transformed a campaign effort into FactPostNews. In the run up to the 2026 midterms, FactPostNews accounts across social media dug up embarrassing and problematic video clips of Trump and the Republicans, presented them through a factual lens that nonetheless advanced the party line, and created a network of creators to disseminate them. As Denny Carter said today in Liberal Currents: “Everything was designed to make Democrats look good and Republicans look bad — you know, the very point of effective propaganda.”

This is a big step for the Democratic National Committee. In the past, it was fearful and controlling. It was scared of what free agents might do to the party’s message if given leeway. Most resources went into making TV ads that have increasingly limited effect. Indeed, that's still the case. But the DNC’s embrace of propaganda is a welcomed development – and overdue. Liberal democracy does not speak for itself nor does it tell its own stories. “People only understand the world through stories. So give them one: Democracy vs. autocracy, dignity vs. oppression, constitutional rule of law vs. totalitarian lawlessness, good vs. evil," Carter said. “These are stories, I think, that need to be told by whatever means necessary.”

That said, it’s not enough. The Democrats might get good at liberal psyops, which for the time being might help democracy more than harm it. But in the end, propaganda is still the GOP’s game, because the vehicle that carries all forms of propaganda – whether rightwing or liberal – is theirs. They spent 60 years building the rightwing media apparatus. They invested billions. They created a vast information and surveillance structure that is increasingly concentrated in the hands of a few, with the pace of concentration accelerating with the integration of artificial intelligence technology. The Republicans own home field. (They own all the fields!) The Democrats are visiting. If they hope to change the game, the Democrats must change the rules, and the way to do that is by enacting and enforcing anti-trust law.

Look at it this way. Before the 2024 election, the Joe Biden administration took aim at Apple in a lawsuit alleging abuse of its phone monopoly. That move came after lawsuits were filed against Amazon and Google, both alleging unfair market dominance. And those lawsuits followed a slew of executive orders by Biden that focused on anti-competitive practices across the economy. “Capitalism without competition isn't capitalism,” the former president frequently said. “It's exploitation.” As for AI, Biden was no fool. It showed great promise, he said. It could help cure cancer. But it also posed great peril to privacy, national security, free and fair elections, and the public trust. His ordered his administration to draw up and enforce rules to set limits on AI while harnessing its potential. From the monopolists' view, however, Biden was gearing up to control their ambitions and suppress their profits, and Kamala Harris would pick up where he left off. They reacted by lifting prior constraints on their platforms under the guise of protecting free speech. Barack Obama and Hillary Clinton faced their share of bile and hatred but that was nothing compared to what the vice president faced. "Such claims are now turbocharged, fueled by an increasingly aggressive tone of political speech endorsed by top politicians, powered by artificial intelligence and other new technologies, and let loose across a far more fragmented online landscape crowded with unmoderated platforms," the Times reported in July 2024.

The monopolists got what they wanted. Trump scrapped Biden's AI rules and allowed his antitrust agenda to stall out. He aligned himself with Silicon Valley to trigger a build out of AI infrastructure that has been so massive that it's currently floating an economy that is otherwise struggling to grow in the face of war-related inflation and high energy prices. (This week, Anthropic's IPO was the biggest in Wall Street history.) In two years, the data centers that power AI went from barely visible to extremely visible. The 2026 midterms were an across-the-board backlash against the monopolists nearly as much as they were against the president. (One advocacy called them "the first AI and tech accountability election.") 

If there’s any doubt, look at their behavior. Elon Musk, who spent half a billion dollars on Republican candidates, now says he was never maga. Alex Karp, the head of AI surveillance firm Palantir, now says he was always progressive. Sam Altman is talking up “human-first” messaging amid the data-center revolt. Ditto for Jeff Bezos. Experts expect him to hype “green energy” to divert attention from his data centers poisoning the environment. The CEOs of Apple and Google appear to have bribed the president into giving them tariff carveouts. They are expected to return to themes of privacy, diversity and not being evil. Nvidia is awash in scandal, as its former CEO seems to have colluded with the Chinese Communist Party to undermine US security. Expect to hear more about Nvidia’s progressive values. (As I was writing this, the Post reported that the Trump administration approved sales of Nvidia's AI chip technology to China in exchange for "for a cut of the revenue.")

The backpedaling suggests the monopolists are worried about the Democrats smashing their fiefdoms and draining their power. Congressman Jamie Raskin introduced in October the Antitrust Accountability and Transparency Act. The objective is “restoring the idea that antitrust enforcement must serve the people – not conglomerates and special interests with beltway lobbyists,” he said. Raskin will be House Judiciary chairman in January. Senator Chris Van Hollen, who is running for Senate majority leader, said a bipartisan antitrust bill that was tabled in 2022 would be “No 1” on his to-do list. Other congressional Democrats are preparing to flood the zone with AI-related legislation to protect consumers, lower prices and secure public trust. These are aspects of a broader trend that Chuck Babbage calls a “techlash.” “How do we tame the corporate monsters to the point where they can be held accountable for making these destructive products?” he wrote in Liberal Currents. “And here are two answers: by wielding the tools of product liability law and antitrust reform.”

The Democrats have no choice right now. They must play the propaganda game, according to rules already established. But propaganda is a means to an end, not the end itself, and that should come as a relief. Liberals prefer open combat between competing values, not covert ops through shadowy channels. By using the hammer and tongs of antitrust law and the regulatory state, the Democrats can change the game so no one solely owns the field.
